    Important Words
    • su-saṁrabdhāḥ — greatly angered
      Compound of su (intense) + saṁrabdha (enraged). The kings' fury is the natural reaction of the materially-proud when Kṛṣṇa quietly removes what they think is theirs — a recurring Bhāgavatam shape (Kaṁsa, Jarāsandha, Śiśupāla).
    • dhṛta — holding
      Past participle of √dhṛ. The kings 'hold' their bows; in the next chapters Kṛṣṇa 'holds' Rukmiṇī. The same root names the act of māyā holding souls and Kṛṣṇa being held by His devotees (dhṛta-pāṇiḥ at Yaśodā's churn).
    • kārmukāḥ — bows
      Plural — the multiplicity of bows lifted against one Lord. Gauḍīyas read the scene as a foil: the world's many weapons against the one Govinda who needs no weapon to win His own.
    • balaiḥ — with armies
      Plural instrumental of bala. The verse stacks military force on military force; the rasa of the chapter depends on this preposterous asymmetry between armed kings and the unarmed cowherd who carries the bride.
    • anvīyuḥ — they followed
      Imperfect of anu-√i, 'to follow after'. The same verb-shape the Bhāgavatam uses for the gopīs following Kṛṣṇa into the rāsa — here it names the opposite movement: the envious pursuing what they hate, instead of the loving pursuing what they love.
    Śukadeva Gosvāmī said: Having thus spoken, all those infuriated kings donned their armor and mounted their conveyances. Each king, bow in hand, was surrounded by his own army as he went after Lord Kṛṣṇa.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Śukadeva Gosvāmī said: Having thus spoken, all those infuriated kings donned their armor and mounted their conveyances. Each king, bow in hand, was surrounded by his own army as he went after Lord Kṛṣṇa.
    Commentary

    This chapter describes the defeat of Jarasandha and others, the disfiguring of Rukmi, consolation of Rukmini and the wedding of Krsna and Rukmini in Dvaraka.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    They mounted elephants and other conveyances. When they had fainted they had dropped their weapons and fell on the ground. Now they took up their bows and mounted their elephants again.

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    Like clouds boiling up around a mountain, the rival kings darken the sky with their armies — yet the mountain (Kṛṣṇa) holds the form of Rukmiṇī under His arm and does not flinch. The fury of the world is the backdrop against which Bhagavān's tenderness for His devotee is photographed.

    Important Words
    • yādava-anīka — of the Yādava army
      Compound: yādava (descendants of Yadu) + anīka (army). The Yadus are the dynasty Kṛṣṇa graced by birth; in Gauḍīya understanding 'Yādava' designates not race but those whom Bhagavān has made His own household.
    • yūtha-paḥ — the officers / herd-leaders
      Yūtha-pa literally means 'leader of a herd' — the same word used in Canto 8 for Gajendra's elephant lordship. Even military leadership, in the Bhāgavatam, is described in vraja-tinted pastoral vocabulary.
    • sammukhāḥ — directly facing
      Sam (together, fully) + mukha (face). Facing the enemy is a soldier's dharma; turning the face toward Kṛṣṇa (kṛṣṇa-sammukhya) is the soul's. The Yādavas demonstrate both at once.
    • visphūrjya — twanging
      Onomatopoeic root √sphūrj — the sound of bow-string drawn taut. Vyāsa is meticulous about the soundscape of līlā: the twang here is a sonic counter to the conches that will sound at the wedding.
    • rājan — O King (Parīkṣit)
      Vocative. Śukadeva keeps calling Parīkṣit back into the frame — the dying king who has only seven days left needs the reassurance that Kṛṣṇa's people stand firm even against overwhelming odds.
    The commanders of the Yādava army, seeing the enemy racing to attack, turned to face them and stood firm, O King, twanging their bows.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The commanders of the Yādava army, seeing the enemy racing to attack, turned to face them and stood firm, O King, twanging their bows.
    Commentary

    Seeing the enemy pursue them, they drew their bows (visphujya) and faced them.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Those (te) who were famous as commanders of the Yādava armies, who had gathered with Balarāma previously in anticipation of a fight, faced the enemy. They drew their extraordinary (sva) bows.

    Important Words
    • śara-varṣāṇi — rains of arrows
      Compound: śara (arrow) + varṣa (rain, downpour). Sanskrit poetics has a stock metaphor for battle-fury as monsoon; Vyāsa picks it up to set up the Govardhana echo — rain that cannot harm Kṛṣṇa's shelter.
    • meghāḥ — clouds
      Megha is also a stock simile for Kṛṣṇa's dark complexion (megha-śyāma). The verse plays the irony: clouds (enemy kings) pour rain on a hill, while the true Megha (Kṛṣṇa) stands as the hill that takes the rain.
    • adriṣu — upon mountains
      Locative plural of adri. Adri is one of the Bhāgavatam's favorite words for Govardhana (giri-rāja). The acoustic association is deliberate — the verse trains the ear to hear Vraja under Mathurā/Dvārakā events.
    • astra-kovidāḥ — expert in the use of weapons
      Astra (missile) + kovida (skilled). Material expertise has limits; the next verses show that the most skilled weapon-handlers still cannot harm what Kṛṣṇa protects. Skill without Kṛṣṇa is a closed door.
    • mumucuḥ — they released
      Perfect of √muc, 'to release, let go'. The same verb-root that names mukti (release from saṁsāra). Here the enemies 'release' arrows; only Kṛṣṇa can release the soul — Vyāsa lets the pun hang in the background.
    Mounted on the backs of horses, the shoulders of elephants and the seats of chariots, the enemy kings, expert with weapons, rained down arrows upon the Yadus like clouds pouring rain on mountains.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Mounted on the backs of horses, the shoulders of elephants and the seats of chariots, the enemy kings, expert with weapons, rained down arrows upon the Yadus like clouds pouring rain on mountains.
    Commentary

    The shower of Jarasandha’s arrows was like rain on a mountain, completely insignificant.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Seated in their chariots (rathopaṣṭhe), expert at war (kovidāḥ), the enemy headed by Jarāsandha released a shower of arrows. The arrows were spread among the warriors. The showers from horses, elephants and chariots were progressively greater, because of their size. Because they were expert they released showers of arrows as if they were clouds.

    Concepts
    Jiva
    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    Arrows fall on the Yadus like monsoon rain on mountain-flanks — but rain only washes a mountain clean; it cannot move it. The Yādavas under Kṛṣṇa's shelter receive the storm as the Govardhana hill received Indra's downpour: untouched.

    Stories
    Govardhana under Indra's deluge

    When Indra unleashed seven days of cataclysmic rain on Vraja, Kṛṣṇa lifted Govardhana on His little finger and made the hill itself an umbrella. Not one cow, not one cowherd, not one gopī was wet.

    The same pattern recurs here: arrows fall on the Yadus like rain on mountains, but Kṛṣṇa is the silent canopy. Gauḍīyas read every later 'rain of weapons' verse as a faint echo of that Vraja morning when the Lord chose to shelter His own with His own body.

    Important Words
    • patyuḥ — of her Lord
      Genitive of pati. Already, before the wedding rites, Rukmiṇī addresses Kṛṣṇa with the bridal possessive — Gauḍīya commentators read this as proof that the relation is eternal, not constituted by the kanyādāna to come.
    • su-madhyamā — slender-waisted
      Su (beautiful) + madhyama (middle). A standard epithet for Rukmiṇī; in Gauḍīya rasa-śāstra it names not waistline alone but the perfect proportion of a nāyikā — the body itself is a sign of fitness for mādhurya-rasa.
    • sa-vrīḍam — shyly, with modesty
      Sa (with) + vrīḍā (bashfulness). Vrīḍā is one of the named sañcāri-bhāvas of mādhurya-rasa in Rūpa Gosvāmī's Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu — the shyness that intensifies, rather than diminishes, intimacy.
    • bhaya-vihvala-locanā — whose eyes are disturbed by fear
      Compound: bhaya (fear) + vihvala (overwhelmed) + locanā (whose eyes). Fear before Kṛṣṇa is not contradiction of love; the gopīs feared Pūtanā, feared Aghāsura, feared Indra's rain — fear directed toward the Lord IS śaraṇa.
    • vīkṣya — seeing
      Gerund of vi-√īkṣ. Rukmiṇī first sees the danger; the next gerund (aikṣat) is her looking at Kṛṣṇa's face. Gauḍīyas note the sequence — the devotee glimpses danger only to be turned more sharply toward the Lord's countenance.
    Slender-waisted Rukmiṇī, seeing her Lord’s army covered by torrents of arrows, shyly looked at His face with fear-stricken eyes.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Slender-waisted Rukmiṇī, seeing her Lord's army covered by torrents of arrows, shyly looked at His face with fear-stricken eyes.
    Commentary

    Rukmini glanced (aiksat for aiksata) at Krsna’s face.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Her waist (su-madhyamā) was bent due to meekness caused by shyness. Seeing directly (vīkṣya) the army of her husband covered with arrows, she developed dears of fear in her unsteady or agitated eyes. This was because she was the best of women (sumadhyamā). They are always timid. Seeing the armies covered with arrows shyly she looked at Kṛṣṇa’s face since she was the best of women or had an innocent gaze.

    Jiva
    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    Like a newly-married bride glancing at her husband during a thunderstorm — fear softened by sidelong trust — Rukmiṇī's frightened eyes already form the prototype for every devotee's plea: I am afraid; You see me; that is enough.

    Stories
    Draupadī's glance in the assembly

    When Duḥśāsana dragged Draupadī into the Kuru assembly and began to disrobe her, she first tried to hold her sari herself. Only when her hands fell away did she throw both arms up and cry to Govinda. The instant she stopped trying and only looked, the cloth became infinite.

    Rukmiṇī's sa-vrīḍa glance is the same posture in miniature: the devotee's eyes turn fearfully to Kṛṣṇa's face, and the protection is already there before the prayer is finished.

    Important Words
    • prahasya — laughing
      Gerund of pra-√has. Kṛṣṇa's laughter inside battle is the same laughter at the rāsa, the same smile while lifting Govardhana — the unshakable mood of one who is the cause of all causes. The smile is the doctrine.
    • bhagavān — the Supreme Lord
      From bhaga + vat — the possessor of all six opulences (wealth, fame, strength, beauty, knowledge, renunciation, per Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.5.47). Vyāsa inserts 'bhagavān' just before the diminutive 'do not be afraid' — the same Person who runs the universe is comforting one frightened bride.
    • vāma-locane — O beautiful-eyed one
      Compound: vāma (lovely) + locana (eye). Sweet-name address. Gauḍīya rasa-vocabulary makes the eye the chief organ of mādhurya — what passes between Kṛṣṇa and His beloveds is, first and irreducibly, dṛṣṭi-pāta, the fall of the glance.
    • tāvakaiḥ — by your (army)
      Possessive 'belonging to you'. Prabhupāda's purport flags this word: Kṛṣṇa transfers the entire Yādava military to Rukmiṇī's account. The Gauḍīya principle — what is Kṛṣṇa's becomes the devotee's the moment she takes refuge — is encoded in one possessive suffix.
    • mā sma bhaiḥ — do not be afraid
      Aorist prohibitive of √bhī with mā sma. The same sentence the four-armed Lord speaks at the moment of liberation in Vaikuṇṭha; the words that calm the gopīs in the rāsa night. Wherever Bhagavān is, abhaya is His native climate.
    In response the Lord laughed and assured her, “Do not be afraid, beautiful-eyed one. This enemy force is about to be destroyed by your soldiers.”
    Purport

    To express His great affection for Rukmiṇī, Lord Kṛṣṇa gallantly referred to His own Yādava army as “your men,” indicating that the Lord’s entire dynasty was now the property of His beloved queen. The Supreme Lord, Kṛṣṇa, desires to share His blissful opulences with all living beings, and thus He sincerely invites them to come back home, back to Godhead. The Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement, introduced throughout the world by Śrīla Prabhupāda on the order of his spiritual master, Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta Sarasvatī Ṭhākura, who himself preached all over India on the order of his exalted father, Śrīla Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura, is broadcasting the loving message of Lord Kṛṣṇa: Remember Him, serve Him, return to Him and share in the infinite bounty of the kingdom of God.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    In response the Lord laughed and assured her, "Do not be afraid, beautiful-eyed one. This enemy force is about to be destroyed by your soldiers."
    Commentary

    Do not be afraid ( ma sma baih). Your army will defeat the enemy." Out of affection form his new bride he calls his troops hers.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Fearless, he laughed to dispel her fear when he saw her in that condition. O Rukmiṇī with beautiful eyes! He exclaimed in this way out of joy, because at this time he experienced the excellent beauty that she had offered to him. They will be destroyed because of your troops (actually his troops). They will be destroyed easily. The plural is used (tāvakaiḥ—your troops) to indicate that his troops were numerous whereas the enemy troops were meager (balam), denoted by the singular. He said this to calm her.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    He laughed loudly to destroy her fear since he was directly the supreme Lord (bhagavān). That is mentioned by Kapila: hāsaṁ harer avanatākhila-loka-tīvra- śokāśru-sāgara-viśoṣaṇam atyudāram One should meditate on the generous smile of the Lord which completely dries up the ocean of tears of intense grief in his devotees caused by separation. SB 3.28.32 O lotus-eyed one! Your eyes have become more beautiful by the agitation of fear. The enemy troops will be destroyed by the Yadu troops related to you (tāvakaiḥ). They will all die. His troops were many indicated by the plural. This will pacify her. The enemy troops is in the singular to indicate their small army.

    Important Words
    • saṅkarṣaṇa — Lord Balarāma
      From sam + √kṛṣ, 'one who draws together' — He who drew the foetus from Devakī's womb to Rohiṇī. Gauḍīyas worship Saṅkarṣaṇa as Kṛṣṇa's mūla prakāśa, the first manifestation of Bhagavān's own self for service — hence His role here as Kṛṣṇa's elder protector.
    • gada — Gada, Kṛṣṇa's younger brother
      Son of Vasudeva by Sunāmā. The Bhāgavatam consistently honors the lesser-known Yadu heroes alongside Balarāma — bhakti-history is not a one-Person show; the entire family of the Lord shares in His protection of the devotee.
    • vīrāḥ — the heroes
      Plural of vīra. Vīra-rasa in Gauḍīya śāstra is one of the sapta-gauṇa-rasas — secondary to mādhurya but real. Kṛṣṇa's pastimes need warriors as much as cowherds; both serve the same Person.
    • amṛṣyamāṇāḥ — not tolerating
      Present participle middle of √mṛṣ. The Yādava heroes refuse to tolerate insult to Kṛṣṇa — this 'kṛṣṇa-aparādha-asahanam' is, for Gauḍīyas, the third of the six signs of śaraṇāgati (Hari-bhakti-vilāsa).
    • nārācaiḥ — with iron arrows
      Nārāca — fully-iron shafts, the heaviest grade. The metallurgy detail is not ornament; the Bhāgavatam wants the reader to feel the weight of what the Yadus bring to defend Kṛṣṇa's choice.
    The heroes of the Lord’s army, headed by Gada and Saṅkarṣaṇa, could not tolerate the aggression of the opposing kings. Thus with iron arrows they began to strike down the enemy’s horses, elephants and chariots.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The heroes of the Lord's army, headed by Gada and Saṅkarṣaṇa, could not tolerate the aggression of the opposing kings. Thus with iron arrows they began to strike down the enemy's horses, elephants and chariots.
    Commentary

    Not being able to tolerate such courage in the enemy, or then not being able to tolerate the courage in the enemy, they destroyed their chariots and horses with arrows.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The word vikramam (courage) is used to indicate the very nature of the enemy warriors, such as the word blue in blue lotus indicates the lotus’s nature. Gada and others could not tolerate the enemies’ courage. Gada is mentioned first because out of great devotion he was in front. Since the horses travelled the fastest, they were first to receive the arrows. The elephants were next. Last, they destroyed all the chief chariots with a desire for complete victory.

    Important Words
    • śirāṁsi — the heads
      Plural of śiras. The head is the seat of vanity in Sanskrit poetics; when it falls 'by the millions,' the verse is staging the fate of ahaṅkāra apart from Kṛṣṇa-conscious surrender.
    • kuṇḍala — earrings
      Ornaments that mark royal status. Their detachment from royal heads on the battlefield mirrors the spiritual point Balarāma will make later (vv. 41–43): identification with bodily decoration is the deepest illusion.
    • kirīṭāni — helmets
      Also 'crowns'. The same word that the Bhāgavatam uses for the kirīṭa of Viṣṇu in Vaikuṇṭha; here, fallen. Royal kirīṭas without surrender to the original kirīṭi (Bhagavān) end in mud.
    • bhuvi — to the ground
      Locative of bhū. The whole verse is a vertical fall — from elephant-back, horse-back, chariot-seat, down to bhū. The motion of pride is always downward; only bhakti goes up.
    • koṭiśaḥ — by the millions
      From koṭi (ten million) + the distributive suffix. The hyperbole isn't bloodlust; it is Vyāsa's way of insisting that the scale of opposition only sharpens the scale of Kṛṣṇa's protection.
    The heads of soldiers fighting on chariots, horses and elephants fell to the ground by the millions; some heads wore earrings and helmets, others turbans.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The heads of soldiers fighting on chariots, horses and elephants fell to the ground by the millions; some heads wore earrings and helmets, others turbans.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The heads fell in order of excellence again from those riding on horses, those riding on elephants and those riding on chariots. The majority fell with earrings etc. though some fell with the earrings and crowns falling separately. By indicating the numbers of dead, the valor of the Yadus is known. “By the millions” is understood with the words in the next verse also.

    Important Words
    • karabhāḥ — fingerless hands (or elephant's trunks)
      Prabhupāda's purport (citing the dictionary) flags the double meaning — wrist-to-knuckle of a human, and the trunk of an elephant. Vyāsa's simile collapses the distinction: the limb of a man and the limb of a beast lie equally on the field.
    • ūravaḥ — thighs
      From uru. The thigh is, in the Vedic Puruṣa-sūkta, the seat of the kṣatriya. The thighs of warriors lying severed are an emblem of kṣatriya-dharma destroyed when it is divorced from the Person who is the original Puruṣa.
    • aśva-aśvatara-nāga-uṣṭra-khara-martya — horses, donkeys, elephants, camels, wild asses, humans
      Six species piled into one compound. Vyāsa flattens the hierarchy: kṣatriya and ass receive the same death in the absence of Kṛṣṇa-consciousness. Saṁsāra is the great leveller; only bhakti differentiates.
    • iṣu-āsāḥ — bows
      Iṣu (arrow) + āsa (resting place, container) — the bow as that-which-holds-arrows. Even the names of weapons in Sanskrit carry the architecture of attachment; nothing in this scene is ornamental.
    • asi — swords
      Asi is also the second person singular of √as ('you are') — and the Upaniṣadic mahā-vākya 'tat tvam asi' famously turns on it. Here the swords lie in the dirt: the Vedic 'thou art' goes nowhere when the 'thou' has not surrendered to the 'That' who is Kṛṣṇa.
    Lying all around were thighs, legs and fingerless hands, along with hands clutching swords, clubs and bows, and also the heads of horses, donkeys, elephants, camels, wild asses and humans.
    Purport

    Karabhāḥ indicates the portion of the hand from the wrist to the base of the fingers. The same word may also indicate an elephant’s trunk, and thus in this verse the implication is that the thighs lying on the battlefield resembled the trunks of elephants.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Lying all around were thighs, legs and fingerless hands, along with hands clutching swords, clubs and bows, and also the heads of horses, donkeys, elephants, camels, wild asses and humans.
    Commentary

    Karabha means part of the hand from the wrist to the little finger.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Karabhā means forearms in the context, though it means literally “from the wrist to root of fingers.” The forearms appeared like karabhas since they narrowed in a similar fashion.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The weapons in the hand are mentioned according to the distance they inflict injury—from close to far: swords, clubs, arrows. The limbs are mentioned in order of the height from which they fell. The horses, donkeys and elephants were carriers of warriors and the camels, wild asses and humans carried weapons for fighting.

    Analogy

    The battlefield becomes an anatomy lesson — hands, thighs, donkey heads, elephant trunks lying together. The verse is not gore for its own sake; it is the Bhāgavatam's blunt statement that the body, severed from its purpose in Kṛṣṇa's service, is no more than its parts.

    Important Words
    • vṛṣṇibhiḥ — by the Vṛṣṇis
      The Vṛṣṇi clan — the branch of Yadus from which Vasudeva and Kṛṣṇa take birth. To be on the Vṛṣṇi side is, in Bhāgavata reckoning, to be on Kṛṣṇa's side; the genealogy is a vehicle for prema.
    • jaya-kāṅkṣibhiḥ — who were eager for victory
      Jaya (victory) + kāṅkṣin (longing). The same word-pair appears in the Bhagavad-gītā's first verses; here, however, the longing for victory is yoked to Kṛṣṇa's cause, not against it (cf. BG 1.32 where Arjuna says he does NOT want victory).
    • vimukhāḥ — discouraged / face-turned-away
      Vi (away) + mukha (face). The exact opposite of sammukha (last verse). Gauḍīyas treat vimukhatā toward Kṛṣṇa as the constituting condition of māyā; here it is dramatized — the demons literally turn their faces from Him.
    • rājānaḥ — the kings
      Plural of rājan. Throughout Canto 10 the rājan-class is portrayed as opposing or worshipping Kṛṣṇa — there is no neutral king. Even Parīkṣit, the rājan to whom Śuka speaks, must choose.
    Seeing their armies being struck down by the Vṛṣṇis, who were eager for victory, the kings headed by Jarāsandha were discouraged and left the battlefield.

    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Seeing their armies being struck down by the Vṛṣṇis, who were eager for victory, the kings headed by Jarāsandha were discouraged and left the battlefield.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Instead of jaya-kāṅgkṣibhiḥ sometimes jayakāśibhiḥ is seen. This means “behaving like a victor.”

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The Yadus desired victory or manifested victory, or manifested Kṛṣṇa (jaya). They were the best of devotees.

    Analogy

    Like jackals who circled a kill but slink away when the lion turns, Jarāsandha and his rank withdraw — not because their numbers shrank but because the protection of Kṛṣṇa cannot be out-counted. Vimukha — face turned away — is exactly the opposite of sammukhya, the devotee's posture.

    Important Words
    • śiśupālam — Śiśupāla
      King of Cedi, Kṛṣṇa's cousin (son of Kṛṣṇa's father's sister Śrutaśravā). Destined to be liberated by Kṛṣṇa's discus at the Rājasūya (SB 10.74). Gauḍīyas read his envy as covert connection — sustained meditation on Kṛṣṇa, even as enemy, ripens into mukti.
    • hṛta-dāram — whose wife was stolen
      Hṛta (taken) + dāra (wife). Prabhupāda's purport flags the over-claim — Śiśupāla had not married Rukmiṇī; the grief is over a projection. Gauḍīyas use this as a parable for material possessiveness in general.
    • naṣṭa-tviṣam — whose color was lost
      Naṣṭa (lost) + tviṣ (radiance). The body's complexion fades when the mind has fixed itself on what was never given. Loss of bhakti makes a similar shadow — the soul drains of its constitutional brilliance.
    • śuṣyat-vadanam — whose face was dried up
      Present participle of √śuṣ + vadana (face). The Bhāgavatam's medical observation: grief desiccates the body. Bhakti, by contrast, makes the body sa-rasa, full of juice (cf. SB 11.14.23).
    • āturam — perturbed
      From ā-√tṝ. Used in Āyurveda for 'patient' — one who is afflicted. Śiśupāla is presented in clinical language; his envy is diagnosed, not narrated.
    The kings approached Śiśupāla, who was disturbed like a man who has lost his wife. His complexion was drained of color, his enthusiasm was gone, and his face appeared dried up. The kings spoke to him as follows.
    Purport

    Although Śiśupāla had not married Rukmiṇī, he passionately considered her his property, and thus he was devastated, like a man who has lost his beloved wife.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The kings approached Śiśupāla, who was disturbed like a man who has lost his wife. His complexion was drained of color, his enthusiasm was gone, and his face appeared dried up. The kings spoke to him as follows.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    By disappearance of color etc., it is implied that eventually he could not move his body, think or speak.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The kings gathered (samabhyetya) and spoke to Śiśupāla after the Yadu victory. Or meeting Śiśupāla, they spoke, since he was intensely suffering, as if he had lost his wife. His complexion was gone. His power of body, mind and words was gone (gatotsāham). His face was dried up. This indicates he could not speak also. The descriptive elements show increasing results of pain.

    Important Words
    • śārdūla — tiger (vocative)
      Tiger-of-men: stock epic flattery between defeated demons. The Bhāgavatam reproduces such epithets faithfully to show how the asurika mind props up its dignity with titles even in its lowest moment.
    • daurmana-syam — depressed state of mind
      From durmanas (bad-minded, depressed). Note how Jarāsandha names depression but offers no actual remedy — only the māyāvāda-style consolation that 'nothing is permanent.' Gauḍīyas distinguish this dry detachment from prema's true equanimity.
    • priya-apriyayoḥ — of the desirable and undesirable
      Dual genitive: priya (dear) + apriya (un-dear). The Gītā's same pair (BG 2.57) — but in the Gītā it is overcome by surrender to the Lord; in Jarāsandha's mouth it dwindles to fatalism.
    • niṣṭhā — permanence
      From ni-√sthā, 'to stand firm'. The same word that in Gītā 3.3 and 18.50 names the firmness of devotional or jñāna-niṣṭhā. Jarāsandha can name the absence of niṣṭhā in the world; he cannot name the niṣṭhā in bhakti that is the answer.
    • dehiṣu — among embodied beings
      Locative plural of dehin. Bodies are unstable; the dehin (the embodied self) is eternal — exactly what Balarāma will spell out at v. 45ff. Jarāsandha touches the truth but doesn't enter it.
    [Jarāsandha said:] Listen, Śiśupāla, O tiger among men, give up your depression. After all, embodied beings’ happiness and unhappiness is never seen to be permanent, O King.

    Translation
    [Jarāsandha said:] Listen, Śiśupāla, O tiger among men, give up your depression. After all, embodied beings' happiness and unhappiness is never seen to be permanent, O King.
    Commentary

    One does not see any permanence (nistha) of happiness and distress.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Śukadeva mocks Śiśupāla through Jarāsandha’s words. He repeats “Bho , bho” to make Śiśupāla, in great pain, face him. It is not proper for a tiger among men to become depressed. Since you are king you should know that the jīva takes many bodies. That is indicated when he says, “O king (rājan)!”

    Like a doctor whose own house is on fire prescribing calm to others, Jarāsandha lectures Śiśupāla on impermanence — the same Jarāsandha who, in eighteen battles, refused to learn the very lesson he teaches.     Important Words
    • dāru-mayī — made of wood
      Dāru (wood) + mayī (composed of). A wooden marionette. The Bhāgavatam will reuse the dāru-mayī yoṣit image at SB 5.6.7 and elsewhere — a stock simile for the illusory body.
    • kuhaka — of the showman / magician
      Kuhaka is a stage-trickster, a sleight-of-hand artist. The world Jarāsandha sees has only the magician and the puppet; bhakti adds a third term — the personal devotee who steps off the stage.
    • īśvara-tantraḥ — under the control of the Supreme Lord
      Īśvara (controller) + tantra (system, controlling apparatus). The Gauḍīya reading: the world IS īśvara-tantra, but Bhagavān runs the system through prema, not mere causality. Jarāsandha sees only the apparatus.
    • īhate — endeavors / struggles
      Present middle of √īh. Material effort always carries the flavor of struggle (īhā); bhakti-yoga alone is anāyāsa, effortless in its essence (cf. BG 9.2).
    • sukha-duḥkhayoḥ — in joy and misery
      Dual locative. The Gītā's standard binary. Material life is, by definition, the field of this dvandva; transcendence is named as 'beyond joy and sorrow' (sukha-duḥkhe same kṛtvā, BG 2.38), which only Kṛṣṇa-consciousness reaches.
    Just as a puppet in the form of a woman dances by the desire of the puppeteer, so this world, controlled by the Supreme Lord, struggles in both happiness and misery.
    Purport

    By the will of the Supreme Lord, living beings are awarded the proper results of their own activities. One who understands the Absolute Truth surrenders to the Absolute Truth, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, and is no longer considered to be within the material system of existence. Since those endeavoring within the material system, or world, are necessarily trying to exploit the creation of God, they must be subjected to reactions, which are perceived by the conditioned souls as miserable and joyful. In fact, the entire material way of life is a fiasco when seen from the perspective of absolute bliss.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Just as a puppet in the form of a woman dances by the desire of the puppeteer, so this world, controlled by the Supreme Lord, struggles in both happiness and misery.
    Commentary

    Just as puppets are controlled by a master, so the jivas receive happiness and distress under the direction of the Lord. Though the demons are here accepting the power of God, they do not recognize Krsna, and therefore they are considered asuras.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    How is this? The example of a woman puppet is used to indicate an attraction for material enjoyment, since the puppet has attractiveness. Nṛtyate should be nṛtyati. All men (ayam) engage in actions. One may claim that happiness comes on its own, and then suffering (sukha-duḥkhayoḥ). This is not true since one sees suffering come on its own also. The Lord is described as follows. Apāṇipādo javano grahītā: the Lord is without hands and feet yet he moves quickly and holds things. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad). Sahasra-śrīṣā purusaḥ: the Lord has a thousand heads (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad). He is like a king. And even if one accepts the Lord, if one is opposed to Kṛsṇa, the para-brahman in human form, all one’s actions are useless. This is the intention of Śukadeva, though Jarāsandha speaks.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Why is everything impermanent? It is the desire of the Lord. To show that the universe is dependent on the Lord, an example is given. Women like to dance. All people (ayam) experience happiness and distress, dependent on the Lord. When the Lord desires a person’s happiness, he is happy. When he desires his suffering he suffers. In happiness he attains what he likes. In suffering he attains what he does not like. Suffering is mentioned after happiness because there is no choice for the jīva. One cannot search out a cause, since it is by the desire of the Lord. If there were some other cause, the Lord’s independence would be faulty. It would mean no supreme Lord.

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    A wooden puppet dances because a hand pulls strings she cannot see — Jarāsandha grants the Lord as īśvara of the puppet-show, but mistakes Him for a remote, impersonal manipulator. Gauḍīyas read the same image differently: Bhagavān is not the hidden stage-hand but the lover who wishes to dance with the puppet once she becomes a person.

    Stories
    Prahlāda on the Lord as cause

    Prahlāda's prayers in Canto 7 echo Jarāsandha's metaphor but invert its mood. He too declares the Lord the cause of all dancing — but Prahlāda's tone is wonder, not resignation: he addresses the puppeteer as 'my Lord, my father, my friend.'

    Gauḍīyas note: the same theological claim (īśvara-tantraḥ) becomes either fatalism or prayer depending on whether the speaker has begun bhakti. Doctrine without rasa is half-truth.

    Important Words
    • śaureḥ — with Kṛṣṇa (lit. of the descendant of Śūra)
      Genitive of Śauri — Kṛṣṇa as Vasudeva's son, Vasudeva being Śūrasena's son. Patronymics in the Bhāgavatam quietly insist on the personal lineage of God: Bhagavān has parents, an ancestry, a household.
    • sapta-daśa — seventeen
      The famous number of Jarāsandha's defeats. Vyāsa preserves the count because the absurd ratio (17:1) is itself the doctrinal point — the demon can win once when the Lord chooses to lose.
    • saṁyugāni — battles
      Sam (together) + yuga (joining). A 'meeting' or 'joining-with' — Sanskrit's idiom for battle is meeting, an unintended echo of bhakti, which is also a sam-yoga but in love, not arms.
    • parājitaḥ — defeated
      Para (other, opposite) + ajita (un-conquered). 'Conquered by the other.' The same word, in another mood, is what every devotee should be: para-ajita, conquered by the Other who is Kṛṣṇa.
    • ekam — one (only)
      Numerical: one. The arithmetic is the rasa — one victory swallowed by seventeen defeats. The verse uses bookkeeping to mock the asurika project of competing with Kṛṣṇa.
    In battle with Kṛṣṇa I and my twenty-three armies lost seventeen times; only once did I defeat Him.
    Purport

    Jarāsandha offers his own life as an example of the inevitable happiness and distress of this material world.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    In battle with Kṛṣṇa I and my twenty-three armies lost seventeen times; only once did I defeat Him.
    Commentary

    I have been defeated in seventeen battles using twenty three auksahinis of soldiers. And in one battle at the end I was victorious.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Though they gathered and spoke to Śiśupāla he did not give up his depression. Jarāsandha then consoled him by citing his personal experience. I was defeated even with twenty-three akṣauhiṇīs. This is well known (vai). The possessive (śaureḥ) is used to indicate the instrumental śaurena. I was defeated by the son of a warrior (śaureḥ). He hides the fact that Kṛṣṇa is the Supreme Lord out of pride. To protect his pride he says “I defeated him once.”

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    Like a gambler boasting that he once won a hand to console himself for seventeen losses, Jarāsandha cites his single victory over Kṛṣṇa as if it proved anything. The Lord allows such victories — they are part of His līlā, never of His limits.

    Stories
    Kṛṣṇa's 'defeat' by Jarāsandha

    In SB 10.50–52, Kṛṣṇa repeatedly retreats from Jarāsandha — finally setting Mathurā ablaze (or appearing to) and leading the Yadus to Dvārakā. From a worldly view, Kṛṣṇa lost. From the Bhāgavatam's view, He chose the appearance of defeat to teach His devotees the strategic patience of bhakti — sometimes the Lord retreats so that the devotees may be moved to a higher, sweeter place.

    Jarāsandha mistakes a līlā-retreat for an actual loss. He never grasps that what he calls his one 'victory' was Kṛṣṇa's gift, designed to set up the founding of Dvārakā where this very wedding now unfolds.

    Important Words
    • kālena — by time
      Instrumental of kāla. In Gauḍīya theology, kāla is Kṛṣṇa's energy (cf. BG 11.32 'kālo 'smi'); naming time without naming the Person who IS time is to glance at the shadow and miss the body.
    • daiva — fate / providence
      From deva. Originally 'that which pertains to the gods.' The Bhāgavatam uses daiva as the residual karmic momentum that the Lord administers — not blind, but personal. Jarāsandha takes it as blind.
    • vidrāvitam — driven
      Past participle of vi-√dru, 'driven, made to run.' The world is driven; the devotee, by contrast, walks with the Lord (cf. Prahlāda 7.5.32, 'where the unsought guidance of Bhagavān becomes one's path').
    • na śocāmi — I do not lament
      BG 2.11 begins with the same prohibition: 'aśocyān anvaśocas tvam' — 'you grieve for those not to be grieved for.' Kṛṣṇa offers the cure (surrender); Jarāsandha offers only the discipline of refusal.
    • jagat — the world
      From √gam — 'that which goes / is in motion.' The world is constitutively motion, never rest. The only rest is in the unmoving Mover, Kṛṣṇa — a doctrine Jarāsandha is one step short of seeing.
    But still I never lament or rejoice, because I know this world is driven by time and fate.
    Purport

    Having stated that the Supreme Lord controls this world, Jarāsandha explains the specific method of control. It should be remembered that in the Vedic context kāla, or time, does not refer merely to a system of measuring planetary movements such as days, weeks, months and years but rather to the way things are being moved. Everything is moving according to its destiny, and this destiny is also described as “time,” since everyone’s destiny is revealed and imposed by the movements of time.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    But still I never lament or rejoice, because I know this world is driven by time and fate.
    Commentary

    Time, under the direction of fate, agitates this world.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    He gives the conclusion. I never lament in defeat. I never rejoice in victory. Karhicit should be understood with both statements. I know the world is agitated by time. “Since time is equal everywhere there should be no appearance of happiness or sorrow.” Time is linked with karma, which gives various results to various people. Previously he said it was the will of the Lord. Now he says it is time endowed with karma. Because the karma of the jīva has not beginning at all, it has no end. A particular aspect of time, composed of the Lord’s actions, produces the particulars of karma.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    He gives the conclusion. I never lament in defeat. I never rejoice in victory. Karhicit should be understood with both statements. I know the world is agitated by time. “Since time is equal everywhere, there should be no appearance of happiness or sorrow.” Time is linked with karma, which gives various results to various people. Previously he said it was the will of the Lord. Now he says it is time endowed with karma (daiva). One cannot find another cause. Or time is related to the Lord (kālena daiva-yuktena). It is under his control.

    Important Words
    • phalgu-tantraiḥ — with a meager entourage
      Phalgu (insignificant, faint) + tantra (apparatus, entourage). The same root phalgu is the name of the dry river at Gayā — externally small, internally sacred. The Yadus look phalgu, but house the Lord.
    • kṛṣṇa-pālitaiḥ — protected by Kṛṣṇa
      Kṛṣṇa + pālita (protected). The exact phrase that defines a devotee: not by self-strength but by Kṛṣṇa's pālana. Cf. BG 9.22, 'yoga-kṣemaṁ vahāmy aham.' This is the verse's secret theology, hidden in an enemy's lament.
    • vīra-yūtha-pa-yūtha-pāḥ — leaders of leaders of heroes
      Triple compound: vīra (hero) + yūthapa (leader) + yūthapa (leader again). Kings of kings of warriors. The grammatical pile-up of titles only sharpens the irony — all these stacked dignities defeated by Kṛṣṇa's 'few.'
    • parājitāḥ — defeated
      Same word as v. 13 — but now in the plural, owned by all the kings. The repetition is Vyāsa underscoring: this is not Jarāsandha's quirk; it is the universal asurika condition.
    • yadubhiḥ — by the Yadus
      Instrumental plural. Even when Kṛṣṇa Himself fights, the credit is given to His devotees. That is Bhagavān's signature courtesy — the Lord makes His servants the apparent agents.
    And now all of us, great commanders of military leaders, have been defeated by the Yadus and their small entourage, who are protected by Kṛṣṇa.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    And now all of us, great commanders of military leaders, have been defeated by the Yadus and their small entourage, who are protected by Kṛṣṇa.
    Commentary

    I was defeated by the Yadus who had meager troops.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Summarizing, he hides his real shame and suffering. You can see this effect operating now (adhunāpi). He speaks in the plural to indicate all the warriors present, or this verse can be spoken by all the warriors. All of us have been defeated. In this verse he uses the name Kṛṣṇa in order to show disrespect.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    All the kings speak together to comfort him since it is later said that ḥe was persuaded by his friends. We were defeated. Or Jarāsandha speaks but indicates all the kings present. Though we were leaders of leaders of armies—most valorous, we were defeated by the Yadus protected by the son of a cowherd. This indicates the Yadus’ inferior status.

    Important Words
    • kāle — in time
      Locative of kāla. Jarāsandha keeps invoking time. The Bhāgavatam will reveal at SB 11.7.48 that 'I, time' is one of Kṛṣṇa's own self-descriptions — the demons unwittingly name their conqueror.
    • ātma-anusārīṇi — favoring them (lit. following the self)
      Ātma (self) + anusārin (following). Demons construe time as serving their self-interest in cycles; Vaiṣṇavas know time follows Kṛṣṇa, not the asura's plans.
    • pradakṣiṇaḥ — turned toward us (lit. moving to the right / auspicious)
      Pra (forward) + dakṣiṇa (right, south, auspicious). The word that names temple-circumambulation. Jarāsandha hopes time will 'circumambulate' him as if HE were the deity — a precise inversion of bhakti.
    • vijeṣyāmaḥ — we shall conquer
      Future of vi-√ji. The same verb that produces 'jaya.' The demons project conquest into the future because the present has refused them. Gauḍīyas note: bhakti never postpones — 'yatra yatra mano dehī tatra tatra samāhitam' (BG 6.26).
    • ripavaḥ — enemies
      Plural of ripu. Naming Kṛṣṇa as 'enemy' is the demon's freedom; the devotee names Him 'mine.' Same Lord, different relation; entirely different fate.
    Now our enemies have conquered because time favors them, but in the future, when time is auspicious for us, we shall conquer.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Now our enemies have conquered because time favors them, but in the future, when time is auspicious for us, we shall conquer.
    Commentary

    When time becomes favorable to us, then we win.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    He uses his philosophy to pacify Śiśupāla. When time is favorable to ourselves (ātma), we will defeat them more soundly (vi—jeṣyāmaḥ) than they have conquered us now. Some versions have vayam ca which means “we also.”

    Important Words
    • prabodhitaḥ — persuaded / awakened
      Past participle of pra-√budh. The verb of 'awakening,' but used here for political consolation. Vyāsa is wry: real prabodha is the awakening of the soul to Kṛṣṇa, which Jarāsandha cannot give Śiśupāla because he himself does not have it.
    • caidyaḥ — Śiśupāla (descendant of Cedi)
      Patronymic referring to the Cedi line. The Bhāgavatam will spend SB 10.74 on his liberation by Kṛṣṇa's cakra — a famous moment of dveṣa-bhakti culminating in mukti.
    • mitraiḥ — by his friends
      Plural instrumental of mitra. The asurika 'friend' (Jarāsandha) keeps Śiśupāla in saṁsāra; the Vaiṣṇava 'friend' (Uddhava, Akrūra, Nārada) draws his hearer to Kṛṣṇa. Both are called mitra; only one is suhṛt.
    • hata-śeṣāḥ — those who remained from the killed
      Hata (killed) + śeṣa (remainder). The remainder — the not-yet-killed — is everyone alive. The Bhāgavatam constantly reminds us we are all hata-śeṣas of Time, and the only question is whether the remaining time is offered to Kṛṣṇa.
    • puram — to his city
      Each man retreats to his own pura, his own walled identity. The opposite movement, which the next chapters will show, is to leave one's pura and enter Kṛṣṇa's pura, Dvārakā — exchange of cities is exchange of selves.
    Śukadeva Gosvāmī said: Thus persuaded by his friends, Śiśupāla took his followers and went back to his capital. The surviving warriors also returned to their respective cities.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Śukadeva Gosvāmī said: Thus persuaded by his friends, Śiśupāla took his followers and went back to his capital. The surviving warriors also returned to their respective cities.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Those who remained after the others died (hata-śeṣāḥ) went to their cities. This indicates that many died.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Śiśupāla was enlightened by logic and sympathetic words (pra-bodhitaḥ) by well-wishers (mitraiḥ). Because they were friends, he was obliged to follow their words. With his father and others he returned to his city. The remainder, returned to their cities. This indicates that many died.

    Important Words
    • rākṣasa-udvāham — marriage in the style of demons (i.e., by abduction)
      Rākṣasa (one of eight forms of vivāha listed in Manu-smṛti 3.21–34) + udvāha (marriage). For kṣatriyas, rākṣasa-vivāha — winning the bride by force from rival suitors — is dharmically legitimate; Gauḍīyas note that Kṛṣṇa's 'abduction' is the bride's own prior plan via Brāhmaṇa-message (SB 10.52).
    • kṛṣṇa-dviṭ — hater of Kṛṣṇa
      Kṛṣṇa + dviṣ (one who hates). The technical name of a category of being. Rūpa Gosvāmī classifies kṛṣṇa-dveṣa as a kind of negative connection (vipralambha by hostility); even hatred, sustained, ripens. But far better is service.
    • asahan — unable to bear
      Present participle a- + √sah. The asurika temperament. To-be-able-to-bear (sahiṣṇu) is a sign of the brāhmaṇa-Vaiṣṇava (cf. CC Madhya 19.149); Rukmī is the photographic negative of that virtue.
    • svasuḥ — of his sister
      Genitive of svasṛ. Family possessiveness, when uninformed by knowledge of Kṛṣṇa as the original father/brother/owner, becomes a prison. Rukmī treats Rukmiṇī as property; she has already become Kṛṣṇa's.
    • akṣauhiṇyā — by an akṣauhiṇī military division
      An akṣauhiṇī (21,870 chariots, 21,870 elephants, 65,610 cavalry, 109,350 infantry per Mahābhārata) — one of Kurukṣetra's standard counting units. Vyāsa lists the size to make Rukmī's solitary final charge (v. 23) the more pathetic.
    Powerful Rukmī, however, was especially envious of Kṛṣṇa. He could not bear the fact that Kṛṣṇa had carried off his sister to marry her in the Rākṣasa style. Thus he pursued the Lord with an entire military division.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Powerful Rukmī, however, was especially envious of Kṛṣṇa. He could not bear the fact that Kṛṣṇa had carried off his sister to marry her in the Rākṣasa style. Thus he pursued the Lord with an entire military division.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    This verse describes the activities when the battle started. He followed behind Kṛṣṇa since Kṛṣṇa had departed for Dvārakā and had entrusted the fighting to Balarāma and others. Hari-vaṁśa says: ādāya rukmiṇīṁ kṛṣṇo jagāmāśu purīṁ prati / rāme cāsajya taṁ bhāraṁ yuyudhāne ca vīryavān // akrūre vipṛthau cāpi gade ca kṛtavarmaṇi / cakradeve sudeve sāraṇe ca mahābale // nivṛttaśatrau vikrānte bhaṅgakāre vidūrathe / ugrasenātmaje kaṅke śatadyumne ca keśavaḥ // rājādhideve mṛdare prasene citrake tathā / atidānte bṛhaddurge śvaphalke satyake pṛthau // vṛṣṇyandhakeṣu cānyeṣu mukhyeṣu madhusūdanaḥ / Taking Rukmiṇī, courageous Kṛṣṇa departed for Dvārakā. He gave the responsibility of fighting to Balarāma, Yuyudhāna, Akrūra, Vipṛthu, Gada, Kṛtavarmā, Cakradeva, Sudeva, Sāraṇa, Mahābala, Nivṛttaśatru, Vikrānta, Bhaṅgakāra, Vidūratha, Ugrasena’s son named Kaṅka, Śatadyumna, Rājādhideva, Mṛdara, Prasena, Citraka, Atidānta. Bṛhaddurga, Śvaphalka, Satyaka and Pṛthu as well as many other leading Vṛṣnis and Andhakas. He fooled those who were following his path.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Tu indicates a different topic. He could not tolerate his sister being carried off since he hated Kṛṣṇa, the supreme lord (kṛṣṇa-dvit). This shows his foolishness and wickedness. Afterwards, he pursued Kṛṣṇa. Kṛṣṇa had departed for Dvārakā, leaving the fighting to Balarāma and others. ādāya rukmiṇīṁ kṛṣṇo jagāmāśu purīṁ prati / rāme cāsajya taṁ bhāraṁ yuyudhāne ca vīryavān // akrūre vipṛthau cāpi gade ca kṛtavarmaṇi / cakradeve sudeve sāraṇe ca mahābale // nivṛttaśatrau vikrānte bhaṅgakāre vidūrathe / ugrasenātmaje kaṅke śatadyumne ca keśavaḥ // rājādhideve mṛdare prasene citrake tathā / atidānte bṛhaddurge śvaphalke satyake pṛthau // vṛṣṇyandhakeṣu cānyeṣu mukhyeṣu madhusūdanaḥ / Taking Rukmiṇī, courageous Kṛṣṇa departed for Dvārakā. He gave the responsibility of fighting to Balarāma, Yuyudhāna, Akrūra, Vipṛthu, Gada, Kṛtavarmā, Cakradeva, Sudeva, Sāraṇa, Mahābala, Nivṛttaśatru, Vikrānta, Bhaṅgakāra, Vidūratha, Ugrasena’s son named Kaṅka, Śatadyumna, Rājādhideva, Mṛdara, Prasena, Citraka, Atidānta. Bṛhaddurga, Śvaphalka, Satyaka and Pṛthu as well as many other leading Vṛṣnis and Andhakas. Hari-vaṁṣa Surrounded by one akṣauhiṇī or many, Rukmī pursued the Lord. He was capable of fighting (baliḥ).

    Analogy

    Important Words
    • amarṣī — intolerant
      From a- + √mṛṣ. The same family as 'amarṣa' (sañcāri-bhāva of impatience). In bhakti-rasa, intolerance can be holy (kṛṣṇa-aparādha-asahanam, v. 6 above); in asurika hands, it is poison.
    • pratijajñe — he swore
      Perfect of prati-√jñā. A pratijñā binds even the gods; here Rukmī binds himself uselessly, since he cannot fulfill the impossible promise of killing the Unkillable.
    • mahā-bāhuḥ — mighty-armed
      Mahā (great) + bāhu (arm). A standard epithet for warriors — but the Bhāgavatam reserves its strongest use for Kṛṣṇa Himself (cf. v. 33 below where Rukmiṇī addresses Him so). The repetition strips the title from Rukmī and re-grants it to the Lord.
    • kuṇḍinam — the city of Kuṇḍina
      Capital of Vidarbha — Rukmiṇī and Rukmī's birthplace (cf. SB 10.52). Vyāsa names it deliberately; the vow about Kuṇḍina becomes the geography of Rukmī's defeat: he will build a new city (Bhojakaṭa, v. 51) to keep the letter of the vow while violating its spirit.
    • satyam — in truth
      From √as ('to be'). The most loaded word in the Sanskrit lexicon. Rukmī swears 'in truth' to do what is metaphysically impossible — to fight the Person who IS satya. The Bhāgavatam's irony is theological, not just dramatic.
    Frustrated and enraged, mighty-armed Rukmī, dressed in armor and wielding his bow, had sworn before all the kings, “I shall not again enter Kuṇḍina if I do not kill Kṛṣṇa in battle and bring Rukmiṇī back with me. I swear this to you.”
    Purport

    Rukmī spoke these angry words and then set off to pursue Lord Kṛṣṇa, as described in the following verses.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Frustrated and enraged, mighty-armed Rukmī, dressed in armor and wielding his bow, had sworn before all the kings, "I shall not again enter Kuṇḍina if I do not kill Kṛṣṇa in battle and bring Rukmiṇī back with me. I swear this to you."
    Commentary

    Rukmi, being intolerant and very angry, took up his bow. He said, "Without killing Krsna and bringing back Rukmini I will not enter Kundina." Another meaning is "Not having recognized Krsna and liberated Rukmini, I will not enter Kundina."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    To show his great courage he made a fitting promise to all the kings who were listening while he raised his arms (mahā-bahūḥ). He already was wearing his armor. Without killing Kṛṣṇa in battle, without him playing some trick, and without bringing back Rukmiṇī, I will not enter Kuṇḍina. This was because he could not show his face to the citizens if he were defeated. This was like a prediction of the future.

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    Like a man who has bolted the door of his own house with a vow he cannot retract, Rukmī swears in front of the kings — and his oath becomes the cage that builds Bhojakaṭa. Pratijñā made in anger, not in dharma, is a self-imposed exile.

    Stories
    Bhīṣma's vow

    Bhīṣma's lifelong celibacy began as a son's gift to a father's desire — a vow undertaken in love. It cost him a kingdom, but it gave him Kṛṣṇa's personal attendance at his death-bed of arrows.

    Rukmī's vow is the inversion: undertaken in pride, against Kṛṣṇa, to recover what was never his. Vows in the Bhāgavatam are weighed not by their severity but by their orientation. Bhīṣma's pratijñā bound him to Kṛṣṇa; Rukmī's pratijñā bound him away from Him.

    Important Words
    • sārathim — to his driver
      Sa (with) + ratha (chariot). The same word for the role Kṛṣṇa Himself fills for Arjuna at Kurukṣetra. The contrast is exact: Rukmī commands a sārathi; Arjuna receives one who is the Lord. The choice of sārathi defines the rasa.
    • codaya — drive
      Imperative of √cud, 'to impel.' The same root in 'pra-codayāt' of the Gāyatrī (Bṛhad-āraṇyaka Up. 5.14.1). Rukmī uses the verb of divine impulsion to demand purely material speed — a small theft of vocabulary.
    • saṁyugam — battle / meeting
      Same root as v. 13's saṁyugāni — 'meeting.' Rukmī asks for a meeting with Kṛṣṇa; he will get one, but not the one he expects. Every meeting with Bhagavān, even hostile, leaves the asura altered.
    • satvaraḥ — quickly
      Sat (with) + tvara (haste). The grammatical irony — 'with hurry' the very prefix sat-, also names truth. He moves with hurry, but no truth.
    • yataḥ — to where
      Relative adverb. Wherever Kṛṣṇa is — that becomes the destination. Even the demon's grammar bends in this direction. Gauḍīya commentators love such accidents.
    Having said this, he had mounted his chariot and told his charioteer, “Drive the horses quickly to where Kṛṣṇa is. He and I must fight.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Drive the horses to where Kṛṣṇa is, even it is his impenetrable fort of Dvārakā. Why? He should fight with me. The potential mood is used (bhavet) to express his strong wish or to express purpose. Drive the horses so that I may fight with him.

    Important Words
    • gopālasya — of the cowherd (or: of the protector of the Vedas)
      Go (cow / Veda / earth) + pāla (protector). The triple meaning is built into the word. Rukmī intends 'mere cowherd'; Śrīdhara Svāmī (in the purport) reads 'protector of the Vedas / of the earth.' Sanskrit refuses to demean Kṛṣṇa even when its speaker wants to.
    • su-durmateḥ — whose mentality is most wicked (or: whose mind is most beautifully compassionate)
      Su (intensely or beautifully) + durmati (bad-minded; or — read as 'durga-mati' — possessing a difficult-to-understand mind). Rukmī insults; the language praises. Gauḍīya commentary feasts on such inversions.
    • vīrya-madam — intoxicated pride of prowess
      Vīrya (potency) + mada (intoxication). Rukmī accuses Kṛṣṇa of the very thing Rukmī is doing. Projection is the asura's epistemology — he sees his own madness everywhere except in himself.
    • prasabham — violently / by force
      Pra (forth) + sabham (an assembly). Sanskrit's idiom for 'in the open, before the gathered.' Rukmī treats public claim as theft. Yet Kṛṣṇa's 'abduction' was conducted in the open, with the bride's prior written consent — Vyāsa records the slander to make the contrast sharper.
    • niśitaiḥ — sharp
      From ni-√śā, 'to sharpen.' Rukmī's arrows are sharp; the answer the Lord gives him (six arrows, v. 26) is sharper. Bhagavān's response is always commensurate, never excessive, never deficient.
    “This wicked-minded cowherd boy, infatuated with His prowess, has violently abducted my sister. But today I will remove His pride with my sharp arrows.”
    Purport

    Śrīla Śrīdhara Svāmī explains that gopālasya actually means “of the protector of the Vedas, ” while durmateḥ means “of Him whose beautiful mind is compassionate even toward the wicked.” Śrīla Viśvanātha Cakravartī adds that the real meaning of what Rukmī said is that today, fighting with Lord Kṛṣṇa, Rukmī would relieve himself of his pretensions to being a great hero.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    "This wicked-minded cowherd boy, infatuated with His prowess, has violently abducted my sister. But today I will remove His pride with my sharp arrows."
    Commentary

    "Today I will take away (nesye) the heroic pride of the stupid cowherd boy who has forcibly taken my sister with my sharp arrows." The other meaning is: ‘I will have my pride in my own heroism removed today by the sharp arrows of the cowherd boy who is merciful to even the wicked (su dur mateh)."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    What is the purpose of doing this? I will take away his pride in his prowess. How could the honorable Śukadeva repeat such insulting words about Kṛṣṇa, since his lotus feet are worshipped by all the devotees? Śrīdhara Svāmī has given another meaning to the words gopālasya and su-durmateḥ so that Kṛṣṇa is praised. Gopalasya means “of he who protects the Vedas.” Sudurmateḥ means “having a mind merciful even to the demons.” He does this to show that the meaning presented by Rukmī was not appropriate. The meaning is this. Gopālasya refers to Svayam Bhagavān, the subject of the ten syllable and eighteen syllable mantras, representing the Vedas which have no beginning and no end, whose perfect, extraordinary sweetness and powers are presented in his pastimes and form. Why do many people have inclinations elsewhere? He is very hard to understand (sudurmateḥ). I will destroy my own pride in my prowess (me vīrya-madam) by his sharp arrows. His power is shown. By him my sister was taken and all kings will be defeated (prasabham). Or by him I am defeated (me prasabham).

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    What is the purpose of doing this? I will take away his pride in his prowess. The other meaning is this. I will offer my pride with arrows to the Lord, Gopāla, famous as the devatā of the mantra, since he has made me his younger brother.

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    Like a thief calling the rightful owner a robber, Rukmī labels Kṛṣṇa 'wicked cowherd.' Vyāsa preserves Śrīdhara Svāmī's reading: gopāla also means 'protector of the Vedas,' and durmati can be inverted to 'whose beautiful mind extends mercy even to the wicked' — the slander becomes praise the moment a Vaiṣṇava reads it.

    Stories
    Rūpa Gosvāmī on 'reverse' Sanskrit

    Rūpa Gosvāmī's Padyāvalī and Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu are full of examples where an apparently insulting verse can be re-parsed to yield praise of Kṛṣṇa. He treats this as one of the proper exegetical pleasures of bhakti — finding the Lord's name even in the demon's curse.

    Gauḍīya tradition reads Rukmī's 'gopālasya su-durmateḥ' through that same lens, with full credit to Śrīdhara Svāmī's earlier note. The slander cannot stick because Kṛṣṇa's protection is in His names whether or not the speaker intends it.

      Ku (bad) + mati (intellect). The exact opposite of su-mati. In Gauḍīya prayer-language, kṛṣṇa-bhakta-mati is the highest mati; ku-mati is its absence. Rukmī shows what mati becomes when it refuses Kṛṣṇa.
    • apramāṇa-vit — not knowing the dimensions
      A- (not) + pramāṇa (measure, proof) + vid (knower). One who does not know the standard of measure. The Lord is the original pramāṇa (cf. BG 7.7, 'matataḥ parataraṁ nānyat kiñcid asti'). To not know His pramāṇa is to live, like Rukmī, without an instrument that could ever read Him.
    • govindam — to Lord Kṛṣṇa (lit. one who gives pleasure to the cows / senses / earth)
      Go (cows / senses / earth) + vinda (giver of pleasure). The name Brahmā gives Kṛṣṇa at the end of His abhiṣeka in SB 10.27. Vyāsa uses the most affectionate of Kṛṣṇa's names in the moment of Rukmī's challenge — softening the air around what is about to happen.
    • tiṣṭha-tiṣṭha — stand and fight (lit. 'stand, stand')
      Doubled imperative of √sthā. The doubling is the demon's bravado. The Bhāgavatam echoes the same doubling in praise-contexts (jaya jaya); here it is challenge.
    • vikatthamānaḥ — boasting
      Present participle of vi-√kath, 'to boast.' The Bhāgavatam catalogues this as one of the eight āsuri-sampat traits at SB 11.5.8. Boasting is rakṣas in seed; bhakti's antithesis is dīna-bhāva, the mood of being-poor before the Lord.
    Boasting thus, foolish Rukmī, ignorant of the true extent of the Supreme Lord’s power, approached Lord Govinda in his lone chariot and challenged Him, “Just stand and fight!”
    Purport

    It appears from these verses that though Rukmī set out with an entire military division, he personally rushed up to Lord Kṛṣṇa to fight with Him.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Boasting thus, foolish Rukmī, ignorant of the true extent of the Supreme Lord's power, approached Lord Govinda in his lone chariot and challenged Him, "Just stand and fight!"
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Vikatthamānaḥ means speaking badly, or boasting. He was foolish (kumatiḥ). And he was ignorant of the Lord’s glories. Fooling Balarāma by taking another path, he was with one chariot. He called to fight personally with Kṛṣṇa alone in great pride, since he had left all the troops far behind. avasthāpya ca tat sainyaṁ rukmī mada-balānvitaḥ / cikīrṣur dvairathaṁ yuddham abhyayān madhusūdanam // With great pride Rukmī, in the midst of his army, called to Kṛṣṇa, desiring combat between the two chariots. Hari-vaṁśa Govinda means bhagavān who has directly appeared on earth (go). The word Kṛṣṇa which appeared later in the text will have a similar meaning. His repeating “Stop, stop” indicates he foolishness.

    Important Words
    • vikṛṣya — drawing (the bow)
      Gerund of vi-√kṛṣ. Beautiful pun: the same root that gives Kṛṣṇa His name (one explanation: 'kṛṣ' = 'to attract'). Rukmī 'kṛṣ'-es his bow toward Kṛṣṇa; the One whose business is attraction permits the gesture.
    • tribhiḥ — with three
      Three arrows. Note the count throughout this fight — three here, six in v. 26, eight + two + three in v. 27. Vyāsa records the arithmetic to underline Kṛṣṇa's exactitude: each shot answered with precise measure, never with rage.
    • kula-pāṁsana — O corrupter of the dynasty (or: O master and slayer-of-enemies of the Yadu dynasty)
      Kula (family) + pāṁsana (one who reduces to dust). Śrīdhara Svāmī (per Prabhupāda's purport) re-parses as kula-pa + aṁsana — 'master of the Yadu dynasty, expert killer of enemies.' Same insult, opposite meaning. Sanskrit again refuses to truly insult the Lord.
    • yadūnām — of the Yadus
      Genitive plural. Rukmī tries to drive a wedge between Kṛṣṇa and 'His' dynasty. The Bhāgavatam's response is the whole rest of Canto 10 — the Yadus are not only Kṛṣṇa's family but a manifestation of His own internal energy.
    • jaghne — he struck
      Perfect of √han. The verb for killing — used here for striking that cannot kill. Kṛṣṇa's body is acyuta; the verb's force runs into a wall. Vyāsa uses violent vocabulary to display violence's emptiness against Bhagavān.
    Rukmī drew his bow with great strength and struck Lord Kṛṣṇa with three arrows. Then he said, “Stand here for a moment, O defiler of the Yadu dynasty!
    Purport

    Śrīla Śrīdhara Svāmī points out that kula-pāṁsana may be understood as a combination of the words kula-pa, “O master of the Yadu dynasty,” and aṁsana, “O expert killer of enemies.” The ācārya gives the grammatical details that make this interpretation possible.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Rukmī drew his bow with great strength and struck Lord Kṛṣṇa with three arrows. Then he said, "Stand here for a moment, O defiler of the Yadu dynasty!
    Commentary

    Kula pamsana can mean "O defiler of your dynasty" But it can also mean "O protector of the dynasty! O killer of enemies! (kula pa, amsana)." Are Ksanam tistha can mean "Stand there a moment." It can also mean: ara iksanam tistha. "Stand so that I may glance upon you."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    By ignoring Rukmī, with a desiring to incite him further, Kṛṣṇa ignored his call and kept moving. Rukmī then shot at him with arrows from behind. Again he spoke as Kṛṣṇa kept moving. Or when he called, Kṛṣṇa faced him. He then spoke with the pride of a warrior. “Stop for a moment, O enemy!” Or the real meaning can be “Please stop so that I may see you quickly (kṣanam).” Kṣaṇam can mean “quickly.”

    Important Words
    • dhvāṅkṣa-vat — like a crow
      Dhvāṅkṣa (crow) + vat (like). The crow in Vedic culture is the canonical thief of offerings — anyajña-bhakṣaka. Rukmī's metaphor convicts him: it is HE who is stealing what was offered to Bhagavān. Vyāsa lets the slip stand.
    • haviḥ — the sacrificial butter / oblation
      From √hu. The substance offered into the yajña-fire. The Bhāgavatam's quiet doctrine: every devotee is a havis offered into the fire of bhakti — and the Lord is the offering, the fire, and the receiver simultaneously (cf. BG 4.24).
    • māyinaḥ — of the deceiver / of one with mystic power
      From māyā. Rukmī calls Kṛṣṇa a 'māyin' — a deceiver. The word's other meaning is 'possessor of māyā,' which IS Bhagavān. The slander is true; only its valence is wrong.
    • kūṭa-yodhinaḥ — of the cheating fighter
      Kūṭa (cheating, illusion) + yodhin (warrior). Kūṭa is also the term for a Vedānta-paradox or hidden meaning — Kṛṣṇa's 'cheating' is the līlā-strategy by which He attracts His own. Rukmī condemns; the devotee adores.
    • manda — fool
      Manda — slow, dull. The same word the Bhāgavatam will use at SB 1.1.10 to describe the age we live in ('mandāḥ sumanda-matayaḥ'). Rukmī unwittingly identifies himself in the curse — manda is what Kali-yuga is, and Rukmī's posture is a foretaste.
    “Wherever You go, carrying off my sister like a crow stealing sacrificial butter, I will follow. This very day I shall relieve You of Your false pride, You fool, You deceiver, You cheater in battle!
    Purport

    In his hysterical attack, Rukmī displays the very qualities he attributes to Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Every living being is part and parcel of the Lord and belongs to the Lord. Therefore Rukmī was like a crow trying to steal the sacrificial offering meant for the enjoyment of the Lord.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    "Wherever You go, carrying off my sister like a crow stealing sacrificial butter, I will follow. This very day I shall relieve You of Your false pride, You fool, You deceiver, You cheater in battle!
    Commentary

    " Where are you going, taking my sister, like a crow (dhvanksa) taking away the offering. Today (adya), fool, I will take away your pride in being a false warrior and cheater." The other meaning is: "Where are you going, not having stolen from me (me amusitva) your own essence (sva saram), Mahalaksmi? I will steal my sister, releasing her from you, and will take her back to my house, like a crow takes the sacrificial offering. Please break (adya make eat) the pride of this false warrior, myself, who is a fool (manda) and cheater (mayi)." Havih means a sacrificial offering or ghee in the neuter.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    You are like a crow stealing butter. The word dhvāṅkṣa means “having one eye.” The opposite adhvāṇkṣa means “having many eyes.” This ultimately means “having a thousand eyes Viṣṇu.” You have attained Rukmiṇī justly since Lakṣmī belongs to you. If your śakti of māyā goes away, then it is possible to fight with me. You fight justly with rascals like us (kuṭa-yodhinaḥ). I do not fight while facing you. I will give (hariṣye) joy (madam) to you by having you performing your pastime of conquering rascals like me. Or you did not steal (amuṣitvā) my sister who is like the sacrificial offering, since she is your share anyway. But I am like a crow.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Stealing my sister was highly improper, like a crow stealing butter. Śrīdhara Svāmī explains the other meaning. Because of deception, you fight by cheating. The real meaning is “I will offer you my pride. Why? You are merciful (māyinaḥ), determined in fighting (kūṭa-yodhinaḥ).”

    Analogy

    A crow attempts to steal the puroḍāśa offered to Indra in a yajña — the bird snatches what was meant for a god and is shrieked away by all the priests. Rukmī, calling Kṛṣṇa a crow stealing havis, has the metaphor exactly backwards: Rukmiṇī is herself the offering, and Kṛṣṇa is the Indra-of-all-yajñas to whom she is owed.

    Important Words
    • smayan — smiling
      Present participle of √smi. The smile is Kṛṣṇa's most consistent expression in combat. Gauḍīya iconography never depicts Him grim in battle; even at Kurukṣetra He is described as smiling (prahasann iva, BG 2.10). Battle is part of His sport.
    • chittvā — breaking
      Gerund of √chid. Kṛṣṇa breaks the bow, not the bearer. The verse-grammar embeds the mercy: He cuts what attacks, not who attacks. Compassion is built into the syntax.
    • ṣaḍbhiḥ — with six (arrows)
      Six — the number of Bhagavān's opulences. Even the count of Kṛṣṇa's arrows witnesses to the bhāgavata-doctrine. Mathematical signs of grace.
    • śayīthaḥ — (you may) lie down
      Aorist optative of √śī. Rukmī's threat — 'lie down dead.' Viśvanātha re-reads it as Kṛṣṇa's destiny — to lie down with Rukmiṇī on the wedding-bed. The same verb, two ends of the līlā.
    • dārīkām — the girl
      Diminutive of dārā (wife). 'Little girl' — Rukmī's belittling of his own sister. Vyāsa preserves the word to register Rukmī's possessiveness mixed with contempt; Bhagavān will treat Rukmiṇī, by contrast, as the Goddess Ramā Herself (v. 60).
    “Release the girl before You are struck dead by my arrows and made to lie down!” In response to this, Lord Kṛṣṇa smiled, and with six arrows He struck Rukmī and broke his bow.
    Purport

    Śrīla Viśvanātha Cakravartī points out that in fact Lord Kṛṣṇa was meant to lie down together with Rukmiṇī on a beautiful bed of flowers, but out of shyness Rukmī did not directly mention this point.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    "Release the girl before You are struck dead by my arrows and made to lie down!" In response to this, Lord Kṛṣṇa smiled, and with six arrows He struck Rukmī and broke his bow.
    Commentary

    "Before you lie on the battlefield, having been killed (me hatah) by my arrow, release the girl." The other meaning is:"Because you are not killed by my arrow ( me ahatah), do not release the girl." "Why do I need the girl?" "So you can lie down (sayithah) " He does not complete the sentence "with her on a bed of flowers." out of shyness.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    As long as, having received my arrows, you do not lie down peacefully (showing the uselessness of his arrows), as long as Rukmiṇī is not peaceful, having her desires for you fulfilled, give up satisfying her and fight. (Before satisfying Rukmiṇī after receiving my arrows, fight with me.) Kṛṣṇa smiled, since taking either meaning, his words were unfit. Kṛṣṇa released six arrows to strike his head, two hands, two feet, and waist.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Before you are injured by my arrows and are made to lie down, free the girl. The other meaning is strike me, having come to lie down with being injured by my arrows. Or until, being injured by your arrows, I remove my pride, do not remain complacent. Do not free the girl. It is not proper to give up fighting. The word me modifies madam and manda in the previous verse. He criticizes himself because of his pride. Kṛṣṇa smiled. In either case he should not speak in this way. Kṛṣṇa released six arrows to strike his head, two hands, two feet, and waist.

    Important Words
    • vāhān — horses
      From √vah, 'to carry.' What carries us through battle (and saṁsāra) is itself fragile; the Lord can disable our mounts to make us walk back to Him.
    • sūtam — the chariot driver
      Sūta — the charioteer-caste. Rukmī's sūta loses his driver-status the instant Kṛṣṇa's arrows strike. By contrast, Arjuna's Sūta IS the Supreme Lord — the very being whose station is high.
    • dhvajam — the flagpole
      Dhvaja — a king's banner, his proclaimed identity. Kṛṣṇa breaking the dhvaja is symbolic: the public sign of Rukmī's authority is severed. Outer authority falls; only Kṛṣṇa's authority stays.
    • aṣṭabhiḥ — with eight (arrows)
      Eight — number of Bhagavān's primary aṣṭa-sakhīs (in mādhurya-rasa). Vyāsa's arithmetic keeps tapping the reader on the shoulder: even in war, the numbers belong to līlā.
    • pañcabhiḥ — with five (arrows)
      Five — number of the senses, the prāṇas, the elements. Rukmī's response is to strike with five — to fight Kṛṣṇa with the five senses. The Bhāgavatam-vyākhyā tradition reads such numerical patterns as catechetical asides.
    The Lord struck Rukmī’s four horses with eight arrows, his chariot driver with two, and the chariot’s flag with three. Rukmī grabbed another bow and struck Lord Kṛṣṇa with five arrows.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The Lord struck Rukmī's four horses with eight arrows, his chariot driver with two, and the chariot's flag with three. Rukmī grabbed another bow and struck Lord Kṛṣṇa with five arrows.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Kṛṣṇa struck each of the four horses with two arrows, to injure their two front feet. He shot two arrows at the driver to pierce his two hands. With three arrows he pierced the insignia, the flag and the pole. He did this to comfort Rukmiṇī.

    Analogy

    Important Words
    • acyutaḥ — the infallible Lord (lit. one who never falls / never lapses)
      A- (not) + cyuta (fallen). One of Kṛṣṇa's most beloved names, used hundreds of times in the Gītā and Bhāgavatam. Cf. BG 1.21 where Arjuna first addresses Him so. The name itself is a refutation of Rukmī's project.
    • avyayaḥ — the inexhaustible
      A- (not) + vyaya (decay, expense). One who does not diminish. The Bhāgavatam's name for the Lord that emphasizes ontological permanence — Rukmī's bows, by contrast, are paradigmatically vyaya.
    • ciccheda — He broke
      Perfect of √chid. The same verb as v. 26's chittvā. The repetition is itself the doctrine: Kṛṣṇa's act of disarming is not a one-time spasm but a continuous mode of being for the Lord — He keeps cutting what attacks His own.
    • punaḥ — again
      Adverb. Rukmī's 'again' is futile; Kṛṣṇa's 'again' is patient. Same word, opposite moods. The Bhāgavatam's poetic delight is in such acoustic chiaroscuro.
    • acchinat — He broke (the second bow)
      Imperfect of √chid. Variation from ciccheda. Vyāsa varies the verb-form so the prose does not lull — bhakti-narrative resists boredom.
    Although hit by these many arrows, Lord Acyuta again broke Rukmī’s bow. Rukmī picked up yet another bow, but the infallible Lord broke that one to pieces as well.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Although hit by these many arrows, Lord Acyuta again broke Rukmī's bow. Rukmī picked up yet another bow, but the infallible Lord broke that one to pieces as well.
    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Though hit by all these arrows, Kṛṣṇa broke his bow. Then he took another bow. Instead of avyayaḥ at the end of the verse sometimes acyutaḥ is seen. That means he did not move from his place or never failed to be affectionate to his devotees.
