    Important Words
    • hariḥ — Lord Kṛṣṇa (lit. the Remover)
      From √hṛ, 'to take away.' Hari is the Lord because He takes away — sins, attachments, and now Rukmī's weapons. Gauḍīyas read every act of Kṛṣṇa's 'taking' as preparation for giving Himself in return.
    • parigham — iron bludgeon
      A heavy club studded with iron. Stock weapon of the heaviest infantry. Even the densest material is fragile against the Lord's lightness.
    • śūlam — lance / trident
      Same word as Śiva's trident. Vyāsa's understated joke: Rukmī wields a śūla, but he is no Śiva, and the One in front of him is the Master of even Śiva.
    • tat-sarvam — all of them
      Tat (that) + sarva (all). The completeness is the point — not 'most of them,' not 'eventually,' but ALL of them. Bhagavān's protection has no leakage.
    • yat-yat — whatever
      Doubled relative — 'whichever and whichever.' The Bhāgavatam's grammar of exhaustiveness. Cf. BG 10.41's 'yad yad vibhūtimat sattvam' — wherever there is glory, there I am. Same doubling, opposite direction: here, wherever there is weapon, there I break.
    Iron bludgeon, three-pointed spear, sword and shield, pike, javelin — whatever weapon Rukmī picked up, Lord Hari smashed it to bits.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Iron bludgeon, three-pointed spear, sword and shield, pike, javelin—whatever weapon Rukmī picked up, Lord Hari smashed it to bits.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Kṛṣṇa then destroyed other weapons of Rukmī which he took up successively. Instead of śakti-tomarau sometimes śakti-tomarāni is seen. This indicates that he took up many pikes and javelins. The paṭtiṣa and asi, and the śūla and śakti are slightly different in shape. The tomara is a type of śūla (lance). Whatever other weapons he was able to obtain were also destroyed. He who destroys the wicked (harih) destroyed them all. There is a version with ādadhyāt. The meter is irregular then. This version is accepted by many groups. There are various contrary versions in different traditions.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Instead of śakti-tomarau sometimes śakti-tomarāni is seen. Paṭtiśa and asi, aas well as the śula and śakti are slightly different in shape. Tomara is a type of arrow. They are listed from heavy to light items. Other weapons were also used (yad yad). The Lord was he who is our master, controlled by his devotees (saḥ). Though he was capable of killing him immediately, he smashed his weapons.

    Analogy

    Whatever Rukmī picks up — club, spear, sword, shield, pike, javelin — Kṛṣṇa shatters. The verse becomes a catalog of useless arms. So too the soul: whatever it picks up against the Lord (intelligence, opulence, family, scholarship) breaks in His hand. Disarmament is the precondition of bhakti.

    Important Words
    • avaplutya — leaping down
      Ava (down) + √plu, 'to jump.' The same root as 'plava' (boat). Rukmī jumps down to swim a sea he cannot cross — toward the One who is Himself the bridge.
    • jighāṁsayā — with the desire to kill
      Desiderative of √han + instrumental. 'With kill-want.' One of the seven kinds of attachment-to-Kṛṣṇa in bhakti-rasa-śāstra is dveṣa — hostility. Rukmī manifests it pure. Even this connects him to the Lord (cf. Śiśupāla's mokṣa).
    • pataṅgaḥ — a bird (or: a moth)
      Pataṅga — literally 'flying thing.' The same word for moth in the famous 'pataṅgo yathā' image (Kaṭha Up.). Rukmī flying at Kṛṣṇa is the moth-image: cannot stop, must burn.
    • pāvakam — the wind (or, by another reading, the fire)
      Pāvaka literally 'the purifier' — usually Agni. Most commentators here render 'wind,' but the resonance with fire (the moth's destination) is unmissable. Either way, Rukmī is rushing into what consumes.
    • kruddhaḥ — furious
      From √krudh. Krodha is one of the six enemies of the self (kāma, krodha, lobha, moha, mada, mātsarya). Rukmī arrives at Kṛṣṇa armored in all six — yet even so, will not be killed, because Kṛṣṇa is also the merciful one.
    Then Rukmī leaped down from his chariot and, sword in hand, rushed furiously toward Kṛṣṇa to kill Him, like a bird flying into the wind.

    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya

    Then Rukmī leaped down from his chariot and, sword in hand, rushed furiously toward Kṛṣṇa to kill Him, like a bird flying into the wind.

    Commentary

    Rukmī ran directly at Kṛṣṇa.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Because his weapons were destroyed (tataḥ), being angry, he jumped from the chariot and ran towards Kṛṣṇa, like a bird in the wind: he was running to his death.

    Like a moth not turning back even as its wings are singed, Rukmī leaps from his chariot sword-in-hand and runs at Kṛṣṇa as a bird flies into wind. There is something almost devotional in his refusal to stop — but without surrender, the same intensity that could be prema becomes only momentum toward annihilation.

    Important Words
    • tilaśaḥ — into small pieces (lit. like sesame seeds)
      From tila (sesame) + the distributive śaḥ. Sanskrit's idiom for 'pulverized.' Vyāsa's smallness of image (sesame seeds) emphasizes the surgical, almost playful precision of the Lord's arrows.
    • iṣubhiḥ — with His arrows
      Plural instrumental of iṣu. The Bhāgavatam never numbers Kṛṣṇa's own arrows in this exchange — the count is always for Rukmī. Kṛṣṇa's response is unmeasured because His resources are infinite.
    • tigmam — sharp
      An older word for sharp than niśita. Vyāsa uses the rarer term to lift the moment — this is not a chase any longer, this is the verge of execution.
    • asim — His sword
      Same noun as v. 8's 'asi' (the swords on the battlefield). There, swords lie in the dirt; here, the Lord's own sword rises. Gauḍīya commentators love such echoes.
    • udyataḥ — prepared / lifted up
      Past participle of ud-√yam, 'to raise.' The Lord's hand is raised, paused. The whole next verse hangs on this paused hand. Bhakti's interruption is about to happen.
    As Rukmī attacked Him, the Lord shot arrows that broke Rukmī’s sword and shield into small pieces. Kṛṣṇa then took up His own sharp sword and prepared to kill Rukmī.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    As Rukmī attacked Him, the Lord shot arrows that broke Rukmī's sword and shield into small pieces. Kṛṣṇa then took up His own sharp sword and prepared to kill Rukmī.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Tigmam modifies asim (sharp sword). Or it can modify rukmiṇam (Rukmī, sharp with energy).

    Analogy

    Sword and shield turned to confetti — and Kṛṣṇa lifts His own sword to end the matter. The Lord is willing to kill, but waits for the right voice to ask Him not to. Bhakti often functions just so: not as the prevention of consequence but as its intercessor.

    Important Words
    • satī — saintly (lady)
      From √as — 'the one who truly is.' Satī names not chastity narrowly but ontological truth-of-being. Rukmiṇī is satī because she is Lakṣmī-svarūpā; her plea has metaphysical weight.
    • karuṇam — pathetically / with pathos
      From karuṇā. Karuṇa-rasa is one of the eight primary rasas of Bharata's Nāṭya-śāstra. Vyāsa labels Rukmiṇī's speech with the rasa-name — alerting the reader that what follows is to be received as drama-quality emotion.
    • bhrātṛ-vadha — the killing of her brother
      Bhrātṛ (brother) + vadha (slaying). A specific category of sin in the dharma-śāstras (bhrātṛ-hatyā). Rukmiṇī is asking Kṛṣṇa not to incur even the appearance of this. Kṛṣṇa's mercy here is also His protection of Rukmī from a more famous death.
    • patitvā — falling
      Gerund of √pat. The classic śaraṇa-gesture — falling at the feet. Cf. BG 18.66 (sarva-dharmān parityajya) where the surrenderer falls; cf. CC Ādi 17 where Caitanya falls at Advaita's feet. The body's geometry is the prayer.
    • vihvalā — agitated / overcome
      Vi (intensely) + hvala (shaking). Same word as v. 4 ('bhaya-vihvala-locanā'). The frame is closing: Rukmiṇī begins the chapter vihvalā for the army; she ends vihvalā for her brother. The same trembling, deepened.
    Seeing Lord Kṛṣṇa ready to kill her brother, saintly Rukmiṇī was filled with alarm. She fell at her husband’s feet and piteously spoke as follows.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Seeing Lord Kṛṣṇa ready to kill her brother, saintly Rukmiṇī was filled with alarm. She fell at her husband's feet and piteously spoke as follows.
    Commentary

    "What will people think if they know that my brother was killed before my eyes?" She was filled with fear because of this, not out of affection for her brother. The prema of the city women is dependent on public opinion (samanjasa prema, proper love), whereas the prema of the gopis is not dependent at all on the opinion of the public (samartha prema ), and is much stronger. However, one should not worry that the general definition of prema, that it is exclusive possessiveness of Visnu, and no one else, does not apply to Rukmini and others women, since they did not have genuine affection for Rukmi and other demons. This will be explained in detail later.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Somehow by fate Rukmī had become her brother. Seeing Kṛṣṇa about to kill him, she became unsteady with fear out of compassion or because people would blame her. “It is proper to kill such an evil person.” But she was very learned (satī). She considered, “This low fellow cannot do anything to the Lord. The miserable person acts out of ignorance, like a sick person. Therefore it is proper that Kṛṣṇa show mercy to him, since he is related to me, and I have surrendered to him.” Kṛṣṇa thought as follows. “He cannot do anything to me. That is true. But how can I tolerate his desire to cause her difficulties? Though I can save his life on her request, I will always have the desire to crush this person with evil intentions.”

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Seeing Kṛṣṇa about to kill him, she became unsteady with because people would blame her. She fell at the feet of Kṛṣṇa because he was her husband. She spoke pitifully to invoke his mercy or out of fear. Someone may argue, “It is proper to kill such an evil person.” But she was full of good qualities like natural compassion (satī). She has affection because he was her brother.

    Important Words
    • yoga-īśvara — controller of all mystic power
      Yoga (linking, mystic power) + īśvara (controller). Title used at BG 11.4, 18.75 etc. Rukmiṇī invokes the cosmic Kṛṣṇa just when she needs the intimate Kṛṣṇa — the larger title makes the smaller request more credible.
    • aprameya-ātman — O immeasurable one
      A- (not) + prameya (measurable) + ātman (self). Echoes v. 23's apramāṇa-vit. Rukmī did not know the measure; Rukmiṇī affirms there IS no measure. The contrast is the chapter's spine.
    • deva-deva — O Lord of lords
      Same epithet used by Arjuna at BG 10.15. Rukmiṇī, in distress, reaches for the canonical Vaiṣṇava vocative. The Bhāgavatam shows: bhakti has its own grammar of address that surfaces under pressure.
    • jagat-pate — O master of the universe
      Jagat (world) + pati (master). The same compound that defines the Lord's role in the BG (jagat-prabhuḥ, 10.15). Rukmiṇī widens her addressee to the cosmos and then asks for one life — a stunning rhetorical move.
    • mahā-bhuja — O mighty-armed one
      Mahā (great) + bhuja (arm). The same epithet she just feared the use of (the sword in His hand). She invokes His arms TO restrain His arms. Devotional rhetoric at its most exact.
    Śrī Rukmiṇī said: O controller of all mystic power, immeasurable one, Lord of lords, master of the universe! O all auspicious and mighty-armed one, please do not kill my brother!
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Śrī Rukmiṇī said: O controller of all mystic power, immeasurable one, Lord of lords, master of the universe! O all auspicious and mighty-armed one, please do not kill my brother!
    Commentary

    "O master of Yoga, you are the holder of great inconceivable power, while Rukmi is the lowest among the controlled. You are the immeasurable one (aprameyatma) , and he is like an insect among the limited. You are supreme among the devatas (deva deva), and he is the lowest among humans, because he is inimical to you. You are the protector of the universe (jagat pate), and though he is evil, because he is within the universe, he is to be protected. Therefore O auspicious one (kalyana), with mighty arms (maha bhuja), you should not kill that inauspicious person with no power in his arms."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    O Kṛṣṇa, with inconceivable powers (yogeśvara), with unlimited form (aprameyātma), worshipped even by the brāhmaṇas (devadeva)! You are also the protector of everyone (jagatpate). Therefore you should not kill him. He should be saved. Everyone has insignificant powers and knowledge compared to you. You create auspiciousness for everyone (kalyāṇa). Therefore do not kill him. He is my brother and I am surrendered to you. Therefore do not kill him. You should not kill this insignificant rascal as a pastime, since you have great prowess (mahābhuja).

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    O Kṛṣṇa, with inconceivable powers (yogeśvara), with unlimited form (aprameyātma), worshipped even by the brāhmaṇas (devadeva)! This indicates that he is the supreme Lord because he is worshipped for his svarūpa of all powers. Moreover he is the great destroyer of the worlds (mahā-bhuja). Therefore you should not kill this insignificant person. Moreover you are the protector of the universe. “But this evil person should be killed.” O knower of dharma! One should not kill relatives. You know dharma of the devotees. He is my brother. You should not kill him because you are auspicious for the universe (kalyāṇa). Or the first two names indicate that he cannot be understood in his powerful form. Even devatās cannot know him. You are worshipped by austerities. O devadeva! You should forgive all offenses committed since you cannot be understood. Moreover, you should not kill this insignificant, weak fellow since you are so strong (mahābhuja).

    Related lectures
    • BKG SB 10-54-33 - Approaching the Lord - 2024-09-12 New Goloka
      His Holiness Bir Krishna Goswami· 2024-09-12· English
    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    Like a devotee who, in the very moment of crisis, addresses the Lord by His most exalted names — Yogeśvara, Devadeva, Jagatpati — Rukmiṇī softens her petition by reminding the Lord of His own scale. To plead with Bhagavān is to first acknowledge that He is too large to be petty.

    Stories
    Kuntī's prayers in SB 1.8

    When Aśvatthāmā's brahmāstra was about to incinerate Uttarā's child, Kuntī did not first describe the danger; she first named Kṛṣṇa as Master of the Universe, Lord of Yoga, the unmanifest beyond senses. Then she made her request.

    Rukmiṇī's address here follows the same pattern. The Vaiṣṇava grammar of prayer is: stūti first, prārthanā second. Naming the Lord's grandeur is itself the petition; the explicit ask becomes almost incidental.

    Important Words
    • paritrāsa-vikampita-aṅgayā — whose limbs are trembling with total fear
      Triple compound: paritrāsa (utter terror) + vikampita (trembling) + aṅga (limbs). Rūpa Gosvāmī catalogues 'vepathu' (trembling) as one of the eight sāttvika-bhāvas — bodily symptoms of intense rasa. Rukmiṇī's body is in a sāttvika state, even in karuṇa.
    • ruddha-kaṇṭhayā — whose throat is choked
      Ruddha (blocked) + kaṇṭha (throat). Another sāttvika-bhāva — svara-bheda, voice-broken. The body cannot get the words out; the Lord reads the body instead of the words.
    • visraṁsita-hema-mālayā — whose golden necklace is scattered
      Visraṁsita (loosened) + hema (gold) + mālā (garland). The decorative ornament comes undone in the moment of true emotion — Gauḍīya rasa-śāstra reads such 'disorder' as the highest order. Cf. mother Yaśodā's mālatī flowers (SB 10.9.3).
    • karuṇaḥ — compassionate
      From karuṇā. The Bhāgavatam applies karuṇa twice in this chapter — once to Kṛṣṇa (here) and once to Balarāma (v. 36). Both desist from killing Rukmī. Karuṇā is the family-trait of the Lord and His brother.
    • nyavartata — He desisted
      Imperfect of ni-√vṛt, 'to turn back.' Bhakti's most precious result: the Lord turns His hand back. The same root as 'nivṛtti-dharma' — turning back from the world. Here the Lord turns His own action back toward mercy.
    Śukadeva Gosvāmī said: Rukmiṇī’s utter fear caused her limbs to tremble and her mouth to dry up, while her throat choked up out of sorrow. And in her agitation her golden necklace scattered. She grasped Kṛṣṇa’s feet, and the Lord, feeling compassionate, desisted.
    Purport

    Śrīla Viśvanātha Cakravartī quotes the “worldly rule” that one’s sister is the personification of mercy: dayāyā bhaginī mūrtiḥ. Even though Rukmī was wicked and was opposed to his sister’s best interest, Rukmiṇī was compassionate toward him, and the Lord shared her compassion.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Śukadeva Gosvāmī said: Rukmiṇī's utter fear caused her limbs to tremble and her mouth to dry up, while her throat choked up out of sorrow. And in her agitation her golden necklace scattered. She grasped Kṛṣṇa's feet, and the Lord, feeling compassionate, desisted.
    Commentary

    Krsna was compassionate to Rukmini, who was compassionate to her brother even though he was against her, evil, and would have been the cause of her giving up her life (if forced to marry Sisupala), out of fear of the social laws that the sister should be merciful to the brother.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Merciful to her, he desisted. Or though he was naturally merciful, particularly he showed mercy when she, filled with sorrow, grasped his feet.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    She was in a miserable condition because of great fear, lamentation and confusion. This is indicated by the three phrases describing her condition. They are successively intense. He was merciful to her (karuṇaḥ). Or he was by nature merciful, but because she held his feet, he desisted from killing her brother.

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    Limbs trembling, mouth dry, throat choking, gold necklace scattered — and Kṛṣṇa stops. Like a husband who has been waiting for one signal from his wife to set down the weapon, the Lord watches for the body of His devotee to ask. Bhagavān is karuṇa not in the abstract but in response to a specific posture from a specific bhakta.

    Stories
    Mother Yaśodā's tears stopping Kṛṣṇa's run

    When Yaśodā chased the butter-thief, He ran from her — but seeing her exhausted, perspiring, garland slipping, Kṛṣṇa stopped, terrified by the tears that her body made visible (SB 10.9.18). The bāla-Kṛṣṇa who outran Brahmā stopped for Yaśodā's distress.

    Rukmiṇī's body here — trembling, choked, necklace scattered — is the conjugal counterpart of that vātsalya scene. Both moments rest on one principle: Bhagavān is conquered by His devotee's distress, never by His devotee's argument.

    Important Words
    • cailena — with a strip of cloth
      Cela — a cloth, a strip. Domestic material, not a warrior's rope. Vyāsa specifies the texture to underline the comedy: this is now a household scene, not a battlefield.
    • sa-śmaśru-keśam — leaving some of his mustache and hair
      Sa (with) + śmaśru (mustache) + keśa (hair). The 'partial shave' — Indian custom of half-shaving (ardha-cumbana) as social mark of public disgrace. Kṛṣṇa's punishment is exquisitely chosen: dishonor calibrated to Rukmī's vanity, not to his life.
    • vyarūpayat — made him disfigured
      Causative of vi-√rūp, 'to deform.' From rūpa (form). Bhagavān is the Form of forms; He alone has the right to grant or take form. Rukmī's vanity was attached to his rūpa, so the Lord touches exactly that.
    • yadu-pravīrāḥ — the foremost heroes of the Yadu dynasty
      Yadu + pravīra (foremost hero). Vyāsa names the army with affection — these are not mere soldiers but the Lord's relatives. Familial categories of bhakti animate even military verses.
    • nalinīm — a lotus flower
      Nalinī — lotus. The army crushed 'like a lotus by elephants.' The image is delicate: even destruction is rendered in vraja-vegetal vocabulary. The Bhāgavatam never lets its similes wander from its lotus-feet.
    Lord Kṛṣṇa tied up the evil-doer with a strip of cloth. He then proceeded to disfigure Rukmī by comically shaving him, leaving parts of his mustache and hair. By that time the Yadu heroes had crushed the extraordinary army of their opponents, just as elephants crush a lotus flower.
    Purport

    Lord Kṛṣṇa used His same sharp sword to give the wicked Rukmī a peculiar haircut.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Lord Kṛṣṇa tied up the evil-doer with a strip of cloth. He then proceeded to disfigure Rukmī by comically shaving him, leaving parts of his mustache and hair. By that time the Yadu heroes had crushed the extraordinary army of their opponents, just as elephants crush a lotus flower.
    Commentary

    Thinking, "I should do something so that he cannot come and cause disturbance again" Krsna showed his contempt for Rukmi by marking his body with some ugly features to let him remember his defeat and dissolve his pride. He tied Rukmi’s head cloth around his neck, and holding the two ends of that cloth with his left hand, with his right hand holding a sword, he knocked off Rukmi’s turban and shaved off bits of his moustache, beard and hair at the root, drawing blood, so that here and there bunches of hair remained. In this way Rukmi looked completely disfigured.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    He tied him with a piece cloth which had been bound around Rukmī’s head and with his knife cut his hair and mustache in order to lessen his abusive mentality, which should be punished. He shaved him in an irregular manner so that some of his hair and moustache remained. Sa-śmaśru-keśam acts as a bahuvrīhi compound adverb. This is explained in Śrīdhara Svāmī’s commentary. Or sa can be taken as saḥ (he), meaning Kṛṣṇa. Kṛṣṇa (saḥ) disfigured his hair and moustache (śmaśru-keśam). While Rukmī was being defeated, the Yadus defeated his bold armies. Instead of adbhūtam sometimes uddhatam (bold) is seen.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Kṛṣṇa tore a piece of his cloth and tied up Rukmī. Forcibly he shaved him because he did wicked deeds. While Kṛṣṇa did this, the Yadus defeated his armies. This happened simultaneously. The troops were situated far from the city and were unlimited and proud. Or though they were proud and valorous, the best warriors among the Yadus like Balaṛama crushed them easily. This is illustrated with the example of the elephants crushing a lotus.

    Important Words
    • saṅkarṣaṇaḥ — Balarāma
      The name He bears as second of the catur-vyūha (Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha). Gauḍīyas worship Him as the support of all life — every breath, every embodied jīva, is sustained by His function. Hence His compassion toward an embodied enemy.
    • vibhuḥ — the omnipotent / all-pervading
      From vi-√bhū, 'to pervade.' Used here of Balarāma — emphasizing that the elder Self has the same all-pervading capacity as Kṛṣṇa. The Bhāgavatam refuses any subordination of Balarāma to mere humanity.
    • karuṇaḥ — compassionate
      Second occurrence in two verses (v. 34 of Kṛṣṇa, here of Balarāma). The doubled karuṇa-attribution is the chapter's secret: not only do the Lord and His brother both possess compassion, they possess it interchangeably.
    • hata-prāyam — practically dead
      Hata (killed) + prāya (almost). 'Almost killed.' Rukmī has been brought to the edge but not past it — exactly the condition that bhakti often produces: the false self practically dead, the new self about to begin (cf. CC Madhya 8.71).
    • vimucya — releasing
      Gerund of vi-√muc. The same verb-family as mukti. Balarāma's bodily 'release' of Rukmī foreshadows the soteriological release Bhagavān grants. Familial gesture and theological gesture are the same shape.
    As the Yadus approached Lord Kṛṣṇa, they saw Rukmī in this sorry condition, practically dying of shame. When the all-powerful Lord Balarāma saw Rukmī, He compassionately released him and spoke the following to Lord Kṛṣṇa.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    As the Yadus approached Lord Kṛṣṇa, they saw Rukmī in this sorry condition, practically dying of shame. When the all-powerful Lord Balarāma saw Rukmī, He compassionately released him and spoke the following to Lord Kṛṣṇa.
    Commentary

    Balarama took in his own hand the cloth that Krsna was holding in his left hand, and let Rukmi loose from his noose.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The Yadu heroes saw Rukmī in that disfigured condition, almost dead from shame. “But it is not proper to release such an offender.” Balarāma was omniscient (bhagavān) and like Rukmiṇī he knew the suffering of Rukmī and the future pastimes of Kṛṣṇa. Therefore he showed mercy since Rukmī was related to Kṛṣṇa’s first wife. Seeing both Kṛṣṇa and Rukmiṇī, Balarāma, filled with shame, spoke to them both. Kṛṣṇa only is mentioned, since Balarāma spoke to him mainly.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    They saw Rukmī with his shaved heard. Balarāma had a different bhāva from Kṛṣṇa since he was the elder brother (vibhuḥ). Thus he released him with affectionate words. “But it is not proper to release such an offender.” He was merciful. He was omniscient (bhagavān). He knew that if he spoke to Kṛṣṇa roughly and spoke to Rukmī with affection he would relieve Rukmiṇī of lamentation.

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    Balarāma is the elder brother who steps between siblings — for Kṛṣṇa's sake, for Rukmiṇī's sake, for even Rukmī's sake. Like a grown-up untying a knot a younger sibling has made too tight, the Lord's elder Self loosens what the Lord's younger Self has bound.

    Stories
    Balarāma always softening

    Throughout the Bhāgavatam, Saṅkarṣaṇa is the gentle counterweight to Kṛṣṇa's sharper līlās — He carries the milk-pails when Kṛṣṇa steals butter; He stays in Vraja when Kṛṣṇa leaves for Mathurā; here He releases Rukmī when Kṛṣṇa has bound him.

    Gauḍīyas understand Balarāma as bhakti-svarūpa Himself — the very personification of devotion, who acts always to extend the līlā into more bhakti, never less. His untying of Rukmī is theological as much as fraternal.

    Important Words
    • asādhu — improperly
      A- (not) + sādhu (good). Sādhu is also the noun for a saintly person; asādhu is then the opposite — un-saintly conduct. Balarāma uses the strongest dharma-word to comfort Rukmiṇī, who fears precisely such transgression.
    • jugupsitam — terrible / despicable
      From jugupsā, 'aversion.' One of the named feelings in Bharata's catalog (jugupsā-rasa or bībhatsa). Balarāma's vocabulary deliberately escalates — He overstates the wrong precisely so that Rukmiṇī sees her brother already 'avenged.'
    • śmaśru-keśānām — of the mustache and hair
      Genitive plural. The dharma-śāstras (Manu 8.379, Yājñavalkya) treat shaving as a social punishment graver than fines. Balarāma names the specific transgression to make the case look complete; then He moves to mitigate.
    • vairūpyam — the disfigurement
      Vi + rūpa (form). Same root as vyarūpayat (v. 35). The Bhāgavatam keeps repeating the root rūpa — the chapter is about who has the right to give form to whom. Kṛṣṇa formed Rukmiṇī as bride; He un-formed Rukmī as warrior.
    • suhṛdaḥ — of a family member / well-wisher
      Sat (good) + hṛd (heart). One whose heart is good toward another. In Gauḍīya understanding, the highest suhṛt is Kṛṣṇa Himself ('suhṛdaṁ sarva-bhūtānām,' BG 5.29). Balarāma reminds us that even Rukmī, as Rukmiṇī's brother, qualifies for suhṛt-status under social dharma.
    [Lord Balarāma said:] My dear Kṛṣṇa, You have acted improperly! This deed will bring shame on Us, for to disfigure a close relative by shaving off his mustache and hair is as good as killing him.
    Purport

    Omniscient Balarāma knew that Rukmī was the guilty party, but to encourage the lamenting Rukmiṇī He decided to gently reproach Śrī Kṛṣṇa

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    [Lord Balarāma said:] My dear Kṛṣṇa, You have acted improperly! This deed will bring shame on Us, for to disfigure a close relative by shaving off his mustache and hair is as good as killing him.
    Commentary

    "It would have been better to kill him. Shaving him with a sword has made his face ghastly." To console the lamenting Rukmini, Balarama in this way engaged in an appearance of scolding Krsna. However, internally he was thinking, "O most clever brother, you have done what is proper." Becoming satisfied, he then scolded Krsna. Suhrt in this verse refers to Rukmi as a friend, relative, a brother in law. Factually however he is and enemy, not a friend. Therefore the word is used to mean the opposite in sarcasm.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Balarāma addressed Kṛṣṇa by his principal name because of the arousal of affection as his elder brother. It is not proper for the Vṛṣṇis, who are most famous, with you as its crowning achievement, to do condemned action. What was that action? Out of shame Balarāma did not mention it in the beginning. He then mentions it in the last line. You shaved his head, but it is not a small punishment for you disfigured him also. He criticized Kṛṣṇa to pacify Rukmiṇī. He thought, “He can be criticized because he is related to me.” Rukmiṇī then became ashamed for by scolding Kṛṣṇa, she also became scolded. He did this to teach Kṛṣṇa. This was his mercy. That is understood in later verses as well.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    O giver of all happiness (kṛṣṇa)! It is wrong for us to do this criticized act. Balarāma includes himself in this act (asmat). Others can do this, but not us. Or it is an act for which others will criticize us. Out of shame he does not mention the act in the beginning, but later mentions it. This disfiguring him is not a small punishment, but death.

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    Like an elder brother gently calling out the younger before the in-laws, Balarāma reproaches Kṛṣṇa not because Kṛṣṇa was wrong but to give Rukmiṇī room to recover. The Bhāgavatam's note (Viśvanātha) makes the līlā's mechanics visible: Balarāma's 'reproach' is theatrical kindness.

    Important Words
    • sādhvi — O saintly lady
      Feminine vocative of sādhu. Balarāma honors Rukmiṇī by the strongest dharma-title even as He corrects her grief. The Bhāgavatam shows that loving rebuke must begin with honorific address.
    • sva-kṛta-bhuk — the sufferer of his own deeds
      Sva (own) + kṛta (done) + bhuj (experience). 'One who eats his own cooking.' The compound is karma-doctrine in three syllables. Cf. BG 5.15: 'na ādatte kasyacit pāpaṁ na caiva sukṛtaṁ vibhuḥ.' The Lord does not assign sin or virtue; the soul harvests its own.
    • asūyethāḥ — (please do not) feel inimical / envious
      Aorist optative of √sūy with a- prefix. Asūyā is one of the six enemies of the soul in Gauḍīya catalogues. Balarāma asks Rukmiṇī not to fall into even momentary asūyā — the verse's tenderness disguises a rigorous spiritual point.
    • sukha-duḥkha-daḥ — bestower of happiness and unhappiness
      Sukha (joy) + duḥkha (misery) + da (giver). Compound. Balarāma denies any 'other' as the bestower — but the Bhāgavatam reading is that the Lord, working through karma, is the bestower-through-justice. There is no third party.
    • pumān — a man / person
      Puruṣa-singular. The same word as the cosmic Puruṣa. The jīva is a tiny puruṣa within the big Puruṣa, accountable for his own actions in the field He shares with the Lord.
    Saintly lady, please do not be displeased with Us out of anxiety for your brother’s disfigurement. No one but oneself is responsible for one’s joy and grief, for a man experiences the result of his own deeds.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Saintly lady, please do not be displeased with Us out of anxiety for your brother's disfigurement. No one but oneself is responsible for one's joy and grief, for a man experiences the result of his own deeds.
    Commentary

    In order to remove the sorrow of Rukmini, he reasons with her in this verse. "Every jiva must enjoy of suffering the results of his acts. So what is this useless affection for a person who is evil and who acts against your husband?" He gives a hint of scolding to Rukmini.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Though Balarāma spoke to Kṛṣṇa in this way, Rukmiṇī did not give up her grief. He then consoled her directly in this verse. Do not ascribe fault to Kṛṣṇa and others. Do not ascribe fault at all (eva), even if there is cause. On the other hand (ca), happiness and distress are not caused by others, but by oneself since the jīva (pumān) enjoys the result of his karma.

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    Each man is the sole bestower of his own joy and sorrow — a sentence as Vedic as the Upaniṣads and as Buddhist-sounding as the Dhammapada. The Gauḍīya wrinkle: the doer-of-actions remains the soul, but the supplier-of-results is the Lord. Karma is real; impersonal karma is not.

    Important Words
    • bandhuḥ — a relative / friend
      From √bandh, 'to bind.' Family is a binding — a kind of dharma-bond. Gauḍīyas note: only the kṛṣṇa-bandhuhood is unconditional; worldly bandhutva can be loosened (cf. BG 9.32, 9.33). Balarāma works within worldly bandhutva to make the higher one possible.
    • tyājyaḥ — to be cast out
      Gerundive of √tyaj. The same root as 'sarva-dharmān parityajya' (BG 18.66). Cast out from family ≠ cast out from God. Balarāma's lesser tyāga sets the stage for the greater.
    • doṣaḥ — fault / wrongdoing
      From √duṣ. Doṣa is the technical term in dharma-śāstra for an act that incurs prāyaścitta. Balarāma names Rukmī's doṣa to make Rukmiṇī accept that her brother has not been treated unfairly.
    • hataḥ — killed
      Past participle of √han. Balarāma's pithy reasoning: 'He has already been killed by his own sin — why kill him again?' This is the chapter's clearest articulation of karma as auto-execution.
    • vadha-arha — deserving of being killed
      Vadha (killing) + arha (deserving). The compound that the dharma-śāstras use for capital offenses. Balarāma admits Rukmī technically belongs to this class — then immediately commutes the sentence by appeal to relation. Justice tempered by family-mercy.
    [Again addressing Kṛṣṇa, Balarāma said:] A relative should not be killed even if his wrongdoing warrants capital punishment. Rather, he should be thrown out of the family. Since he has already been killed by his own sin, why kill him again?
    Purport

    To further encourage Lady Rukmiṇī, Balarāma again emphasizes that Kṛṣṇa should not humiliate Rukmī.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    [Again addressing Kṛṣṇa, Balarāma said:] A relative should not be killed even if his wrongdoing warrants capital punishment. Rather, he should be thrown out of the family. Since he has already been killed by his own sin, why kill him again?
    Commentary

    Balarama speaks this verse to Krsna, giving him moral instructions, in order to satisfy Rukmini. A relative should not be killed by a relative. A brother in law should not killed by the sister’s husband.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Seeing her still in grief, Balarāma then scolded Kṛṣṇa in order to remove her grief. The relative should not be killed by a friend (bandhoḥ). He should be rejected. This shows that he should be disrespected but cannot be killed. “But if someone kills another person who should not be killed, not killing him is a fault.” He is killed by his own fault. What is the use of again killing this person who is killed by rejection of society, which is the equivalent of death? It serves no purpose. By giving Rukmiṇī to another person he has been ostracized. Disfiguring him is death since it causes more grief than death itself.

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    A relative who has earned death by his deed should be cast out, not killed — like a diseased branch pruned, not the whole orchard burned. Balarāma articulates a careful dharma: there is a level of family-protection that survives even the gravest wrongdoing.

    Important Words
    • kṣatriyāṇām — of the warriors
      Genitive plural of kṣatriya. The varṇa whose dharma includes vadha as a possibility. Gauḍīyas read the kṣatriya-varṇa in Canto 10 as both honored and superseded — honored as Kṛṣṇa's own appearance varṇa, superseded by the bhakti He inaugurates.
    • prajāpati-vinirmitaḥ — established by the original progenitor (Brahmā)
      Prajāpati (lord of beings, Brahmā) + vinirmitaḥ (built). The law's authority is traced to the demigod-creator. Gauḍīya note: even Brahmā's laws are conditional; only Kṛṣṇa's nāma-dharma is absolute.
    • bhrātā-api-bhrātaram-hanyāt — a brother may have to kill his brother
      The four-word pāda joined as a unit. The Bhāgavatam quotes the law verbatim — and immediately names it ghoratama. The verse is the prosecution and the verdict in one breath.
    • ghora-tamaḥ — most terrible
      Superlative of ghora (terrible). The same root as Aghāsura's name (a-ghora, 'not terrible' — he is named ironically). Balarāma uses the strongest negative adjective to flag the limits of varṇa-dharma.
    • dharmaḥ — code of sacred duty
      From √dhṛ. The Lord's bhāgavata-dharma (cf. SB 1.2.6) is the supreme dharma — sva-dharma is provisional. Balarāma names sva-dharma here but the next verses already pivot toward a higher view.
    [Turning to Rukmiṇī, Balarāma continued:] The code of sacred duty for warriors established by Lord Brahmā enjoins that one may have to kill even his own brother. That is indeed a most dreadful law.
    Purport

    Lord Balarāma, in the interest of fairness, is giving a complete analysis of the situation. Although one should not kill a relative, there are extenuating circumstances according to military codes. In the American Civil War, which took place in the 1860s, many families were divided between the army of the North and that of the South, and thus fratricidal killing unfortunately became a common affair. Such killing is certainly ghoratama, most dreadful. Yet such is the nature of the material world, where duty, honor and so-called justice often create conflict. Only on the spiritual platform, in pure Kṛṣṇa consciousness, can we transcend the unacceptable pain of material existence. Rukmī was maddened by pride and envy and thus could not understand anything about Kṛṣṇa or Kṛṣṇa consciousness.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    [Turning to Rukmiṇī, Balarāma continued:] The code of sacred duty for warriors established by Lord Brahmā enjoins that one may have to kill even his own brother. That is indeed a most dreadful law.
    Commentary

    He speaks again to Rukmini who was saying in her mind, "Your younger brother does not know this rule." "One should even kill ones brother. That is the rule of the scripture. What to speak then of a brother in law who is so vile?"

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Since she still did not give up her grief, he again tried to enlighten her by showing sva-dharma of kṣatriyas. This dharma of the kṣatriyas—obligatory action generated by karma- is that a brother must kill his brother in a just war. This is dharma because it has been created by Brahmā. This means it is directed by the Vedas. Therefore (tataḥ) this is a terrible rule since it involves killing a brother. Śrīdhara Svāmī agrees with this meaning.

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    The kṣatriya-dharma, instituted by Brahmā, can require even fratricide — a law Balarāma calls 'most dreadful' (ghoratama). The Bhāgavatam stages a critique of dharma from within dharma itself: even when the rules are followed, they can produce horror. Only the bhakti that exceeds varṇa-dharma resolves the contradiction.

    Stories
    Arjuna's collapse at Kurukṣetra

    Standing between two armies of cousins and uncles, Arjuna dropped his bow precisely because kṣatriya-dharma was about to require him to do what Balarāma here calls ghoratama. He could not bear it.

    Kṛṣṇa's answer in the Gītā is exactly what Balarāma is implying here: above varṇa-dharma stands sarva-dharmān parityajya — the surrender that transcends the calculus of duty. The Bhāgavatam reads BG 18.66 back into BG 1: even the most established duty-system is not the last word.

    Important Words
    • rājyasya — of kingdom
      Genitive of rājya. First of the six tinsels Balarāma names. Cf. BG 1.32 where Arjuna says 'na kāṅkṣe vijayaṁ kṛṣṇa na ca rājyaṁ sukhāni ca' — exactly the renunciation of rājya as motive.
    • striyaḥ — of a woman
      Genitive of strī. Listed alongside kingdom, land, wealth — Balarāma is naming the typical asurika preoccupations. The Bhāgavatam does not condemn women; it condemns their use as objects of pride.
    • mānasya — of honor
      From √man. Māna — false ego, pride, prestige. In Gauḍīya psychology, māna is the chief obstacle to dīnatā, the mood of being-poor before the Lord that opens prema. Hence its inclusion in this catalog.
    • śrī-mada-andhāḥ — blinded by the intoxication of opulence
      Triple compound: śrī (opulence) + mada (intoxication) + andha (blind). Same word that, in feminine, names Lakṣmī (Śrī). The play: those who chase śrī without offering it to the Lord become śrī-mada-andha, blind in opulence's drunken state.
    • kṣipanti — they commit insult / cast offense
      Present of √kṣip, 'to throw, to hurl.' Insult IS the throwing of words. Gauḍīya śāstra catalogues vaiṣṇava-aparādha as the gravest of throws — even more dangerous than nāma-aparādha, since it 'rebounds' (cf. CC Madhya 19).
    [Again Balarāma addressed Kṛṣṇa:] Blinded by conceit with their personal opulences, proud men offend others for the sake of such things as kingdom, land, wealth, women, honor and power.
    Purport

    Lord Kṛṣṇa was originally meant to marry Rukmiṇī. All along this was the best arrangement for all concerned, and yet from the beginning Rukmī had maliciously opposed this beautiful arrangement. When his sister’s desire was finally fulfilled and she was taken by Kṛṣṇa, he viciously attacked the Lord with vulgar insults and mortal weapons. In return Lord Kṛṣṇa tied him up and partially clipped his hair and mustache. While certainly humiliating for a puffed-up prince like Rukmī, his punishment was a mere slap on the wrist, considering what he had done.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    [Again Balarāma addressed Kṛṣṇa:] Blinded by conceit with their personal opulences, proud men offend others for the sake of such things as kingdom, land, wealth, women, honor and power.
    Commentary

    Guessing that Rukmini would be thinking to herself, "It may be true that a ksatriya can kill his relative, but he should not disfigure him in a ghastly way." Balarama then speaks to Krsna to satisfy her. "O Krsna, those who are proud abuse others in order to gett kingdom, land, money, power etc. But we should not do this."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    He again speaks harshly to Kṛṣṇa to console Rukmiṇī. Because of kingdom, land, worship (mānasya), beauty or strength (tejasaḥ) and other things like food and drink, proud people who become blinded by pride and wealth cause destruction. Since (hi) persons blinded by pride and wealth act in this way, we should not do this, since we are not blind.

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    Blinded by their own ornaments, proud men insult others over kingdom, land, wealth, women, honor, power — the six tinsels of māyā. Balarāma's list is a complete catalog of saṁsāra's pretexts for offense. Bhakti does not enter the list because it makes no pretext for offense.

    Important Words
    • viṣamā-buddhiḥ — biased / unfair attitude
      Viṣama (uneven, partial) + buddhi (intelligence). The opposite of sama-buddhi which the Gītā repeatedly praises (BG 5.18, 6.32). Balarāma names Rukmiṇī's attachment to her brother as a form of viṣama-buddhi — kindly, but precisely.
    • durhṛdām — of those who have ill intentions
      Genitive plural of durhṛd. Dur (bad) + hṛd (heart). The opposite of suhṛd. Balarāma's lexicon makes the moral architecture of the situation precise: Rukmī is durhṛd toward all beings; Kṛṣṇa is suhṛd. Yet Rukmiṇī pleads for the durhṛd.
    • ajña-vat — like an ignorant person
      Ajña (ignorant) + vat (like). Balarāma does not call her ignorant; only LIKE an ignorant person. The hedge is the tenderness — He preserves her sādhvī status while still naming the cognitive distortion.
    • sarva-bhūteṣu — toward all living beings
      Sarva (all) + bhūta (being). The cosmic scope. Balarāma reminds Rukmiṇī that Rukmī's ill-will is not only toward Kṛṣṇa or toward her — it extends to all beings. This is the Bhāgavatam's standard of evil: not merely personal injury but enmity-to-all.
    • abhadram — evil / inauspicious
      A- (not) + bhadra (auspicious). To wish abhadra to one's well-wishers is exactly the inversion Balarāma is correcting. The Bhāgavatam's word-pair (bhadra / abhadra) is more about auspiciousness than moral right-wrong — a Vedic, ritual scale.
    [To Rukmiṇī Balarāma said:] Your attitude is unfair, for like an ignorant person you wish good to those who are inimical to all living beings and who have done evil to your true well-wishers.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    [To Rukmiṇī Balarāma said:] Your attitude is unfair, for like an ignorant person you wish good to those who are inimical to all living beings and who have done evil to your true well-wishers.
    Commentary

    "But this rule is for situations other than war. The rule in war is that the enemy should be defeated, and made insignificant." Guessing that this was Krsna’s internal thought, Balarama then spoke to Rukmini with this verse. "Krsna treatment of relatives who have evil intentions to all beings, such as shaving your brother, which you think is wrong for them, is actually correct. It is due to your biased intelligence, like that of ignorant people, though actually you have good intelligence."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Balarāma spoke to Rukmiṇī, enlightening her by means of dharma in order to pacify her. Such instructions were not necessary for Kṛṣṇa. Since she did not give up lamenting, he speaks with anger at first, enlightening her with teachings of jṣāna, containing a secret message for her to have her give up lamenting. Just as you desire bad for those among all beings who appear to show animosity, you desire good for Rukmī and others who appear to show friendship. And to others you are neutral. This is disturbed intelligence, like that of ignorant people. There is another meaning in which suhrḍam modifies duhrdām. Among all beings, you wish bad fortune to Śiśupāla and others who are confirmed as enemies and you wish good to their friends like Rukmī who assist them. Thus you have disturbed intelligence. You should think of them as enemies as well and wish them bad fortune.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Though the words for Rukmiṇī, he addressed Kṛṣṇa. However she did still not give up lamenting. Thus he stopped speaking to Kṛṣṇa and enlightened her with philosophical teachings. You wish good fortune for friends and the opposite for enemies.

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    Wishing well to those who wish ill to all beings, and ill to those who wish you well — this is the unbalance of attachment. Balarāma's diagnosis is gentle but unsparing: even Rukmiṇī's love-for-her-brother carries a touch of ajñāna-vat-buddhi, the ignorance that mis-weighs the relationships of the soul.

    Important Words
    • ātma-mohaḥ — the bewilderment about the self
      Ātma (self) + moha (bewilderment). The original ignorance. Cf. CC Madhya 22.31: 'kṛṣṇa-bahirmukha hañā bhoga-vāñchā kare' — when the soul turns from Kṛṣṇa, ātma-moha begins. Balarāma names the disease at its root.
    • deva-māyayā — by the illusory energy of the Supreme Lord
      Deva (the Lord) + māyā (His energy). Crucial Gauḍīya formula: māyā is HIS energy, not an independent principle. Cf. BG 7.14, 'daivī hy eṣā guṇa-mayī mama māyā.' Māyā is not the Lord's enemy; she is His servant.
    • suhṛt-durhṛt-udāsīnaḥ — friend, enemy, neutral
      Triple compound. The three social positions one classifies others into. Cf. BG 6.9 where the yogi is praised as one who sees all three classes equally. Balarāma is teaching Rukmiṇī to dissolve the distinction by which she has been pleading.
    • deha-ātma-māninām — for those who consider the body to be the self
      Deha (body) + ātma (self) + mānin (considerer). Quadruple compound. The classic Bhāgavata diagnosis of saṁsāra (cf. SB 10.84.13 — 'yasy ātma-buddhiḥ kuṇape tridhātuke'). All other errors flow from this primary identification.
    • kalpate — is effected / takes shape
      Present passive of √kḷp. 'Is constructed.' The bewilderment is not native to the soul; it is constructed by māyā upon a deha-mānī. Take away the deha-māna and the moha collapses. Cf. CC's central pedagogy.
    The Supreme Lord’s Māyā makes men forget their real selves, and thus, taking the body for the self, they consider others to be friends, enemies or neutral parties.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The Supreme Lord's Māyā makes men forget their real selves, and thus, taking the body for the self, they consider others to be friends, enemies or neutral parties.
    Commentary

    "I know that my brother is evil, but thought that is so, still I have some attachment as a relative. What can I do?" "Certainly for an elevated person like you, such bad judement is not proper. But for worldly people this is their natural tendency. For those who think that their bodies are themselves, there is such bewilderment, but not for the persons in knowledge."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    One considers someone as a friend and someone as an enemy. And sometimes one person is considered a friend and sometimes an enemy. Another meaning is as follows. Those who do not experience Kṛṣṇa prema look for friendship elsewhere. That is explained in this and the next verse.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The illusion of the mind or the self produces notions that someone is a friend, someone is an enemy, or someone is neutral by the Lord’s māyā, because people think themselves to be the body. This is all illusion and difficult to surpass. Or this illusion of the self, produced by the Lord’s māyā, causes one to think someone is a friend and someone is an enemy. Mention of enemies and neutral parties is a general statement (not indicating Rukmiṇī’s mind).

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    Like a man wearing tinted glasses who insists the world is red, men under māyā take the body for the self and then classify others as friend, enemy, or stranger on that mistaken basis. The Vaiṣṇava answer is not to remove the classifications but to relocate them: friend, enemy, neutral, all are equally servants-of-Kṛṣṇa, equally to be wished well.

    Important Words
    • paraḥ — the Supreme
      Para — the Supreme. The Gauḍīya reading: paraḥ ātmā here is Paramātmā, the Lord's pervasive aspect, not a featureless 'one.' One Lord, infinitely related to many jīvas. The word para is laden — used in Vaiṣṇava texts for everything trans-material.
    • jyotiḥ — a celestial body / light
      Light of sun, moon, or star. Prabhupāda's purport explicates: one moon, many reflections. The simile carries acintya-bhedābheda — the moon is really one and really many at once.
    • nabhaḥ — the sky
      Nabhas. The sky is one; the sky in a thousand water-pots is one-as-many. A Bhāgavata-classic image. The Lord's presence in each jīva is real (bhedā), yet His unity is unbroken (abhedā).
    • mūḍhaiḥ — by those who are bewildered
      Plural instrumental of mūḍha. The same word the Gītā uses (BG 7.25) for those who do not know the Lord. Bewilderment here = mistaking the apparent plurality of jīvas for ontological pluralism.
    • nānā-iva — as if many
      Nānā (many) + iva (as if). The iva is doing all the philosophical work — the multiplicity is real-as-perceived but not absolutely real. Gauḍīyas insert their bhedābheda exactly at this iva.
    Those who are bewildered perceive the one Supreme Soul, who resides in all embodied beings, as many, just as one may perceive the light in the sky, or the sky itself, as many.
    Purport

    The last line of this text, y athā jyotir yathā nabhaḥ, introduces two analogies in which we perceive one thing to be many. Jyotiḥ indicates the light of heavenly bodies such as the sun or moon. Although there is only one moon, we may see the moon reflected in pools, rivers, lakes and buckets of water. Then it would appear as if there were many moons, although there is only one. Similarly, we perceive a divine presence in each living being because the Supreme Lord is present everywhere, although He is one. The second analogy given here, yathā nabhaḥ, is that of the sky. If we have a row of sealed clay pots in a room, the sky, or air, is in each pot, although the sky itself is one. The Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (1.2.32) gives a similar analogy concerning fire and wood: yathā hy avahito vahnir dāruṣv ekaḥ sva-yoniṣu nāneva bhāti viśvātmā bhūteṣu ca tathā pumān “The Lord, as the Supersoul, pervades all things, just as fire permeates wood, and so He appears to be of many varieties, though He is the absolute one without a second.”

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Those who are bewildered perceive the one Supreme Soul, who resides in all embodied beings, as many, just as one may perceive the light in the sky, or the sky itself, as many.
    Commentary

    In two verse he refutes the misconception of those who think body is self. First he states that the body is not the supersoul. The supersoul is certainly the one inspirer of the many jivas with bodies. Two examples are given to show one is the basis of many. It is like fire within wood and ether in the pot, as is said in the First cantao: yatha hy avahito... The Lord, as Supersoul, pervades all things, just as fire permeates wood, and so He appears to be of many varieties, though He is the absolute one without a second.(sb 1.2.32)

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    “We directly see variety in the universe. So then there should also be friendship in the universe.” How do you say that? This is illusion about ātmā. All the jīvas are spiritual in nature, and thus actually have no difference. They are one only (ekaḥ). As amśas of Paramātmā they all have similar svarūpa. Paramātmā with inconceivable energy is like the sun. The ātmās, as aṁśas of taṭastha-śakti, are like particles of light in the sun’s rays. Since the ātmās are like the light of the sun, because of the inconceivable energy, acintya-śakti, there is no room for raising an objection about them. They are one because (hi) the ātmā is different from the body (paraḥ). There is variety only because of bodies. There is no variety in the ātmā. How can variety be perceived, since the ātmās are all without material disturbances? The variety arises because of variety in the ātmā’s location. Examples are given. In the first example of light perceived as many reflections, there is difference perceived between the object and its reflection. Thus another example is given: the sky in the pot. There is another meaning. Ātatatvāc ca mātṛtvād ātmā hi paramo hariḥ: the Lord is called ātmā since he spreads everywhere and is the source of everything like a mother. (quoted in Śrīdhara’s Bhāgavatam commentary) The Supreme Lord (ātmā) is one only. He is the one ātmā in all those who identify with their bodies. He is in reality the best, superior (paraḥ) to all of them, exhibiting the highest prema. The ātmās, those who identify with bodies, are accepted by fools to be supreme. When illusion dissolves in some persons, they perceive ātmā in its true form according to qualification, with a shadow of prema. An example is given. If one has not seen the sun, a lamp is accepted as supreme. Having not seen the expansive sky, flies take the space in an uḍumbara tree to be the supreme sky.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    “We directly see variety in the universe. So then there should also be friendship in the universe.” How do you say that? This is illusion about ātmā. All the jīvas are spiritual in nature, and thus actually have no difference. They are one only (ekaḥ). There is one ātmā for all those receiving various types of bodies of four types since it is different from the bodies (paraḥ). The bodies are various, but not the ātmā. Why is variety perceived? There is variety in the upādhi of bodies. An example is given. It looks like variety (iva) for fools who do not know the truth or who identify with their bodies, but is actually one.

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    One moon is seen as many in many pools; one sky is perceived as many through many windows. Balarāma uses sky-and-light imagery to teach jīva-Brahman unity-in-distinction. Gauḍīyas read this acintya-bhedābheda: the Supreme is one, yet really plural in the multiple jīvas — like the same sun's rays in many waters.

    Important Words
    • dehaḥ — the material body
      From √dih, 'to smear, to plaster.' Etymologically: 'that which is smeared on.' The body is plaster over the soul. Gauḍīya readers love this etymology — it carries the doctrine in its root.
    • dravya-prāṇa-guṇa-ātmakaḥ — composed of elements, senses, and modes
      Quadruple compound. Three constitutive categories of the material body in Sāṅkhya analysis. The Bhāgavatam frequently encloses Sāṅkhya within bhakti — uses its categories, refuses its conclusions.
    • avidyayā — by ignorance
      Instrumental of avidyā. The cause of the body's imposition. Gauḍīyas read avidyā as māyā's specific function of forgetting Kṛṣṇa; remove the forgetting (via śravaṇa-kīrtana) and the body's imposition begins to dissolve.
    • saṁsārayati — causes to experience the cycle of birth and death
      Causative of sam-√sṛ, 'to flow around.' Saṁsāra IS the flowing-around. The body causes the saṁsāra; the saṁsāra causes new bodies. A self-perpetuating wheel that only bhakti can stop (cf. SB 11.2.37).
    • kḷptaḥ — imposed / constructed
      From √kḷp, 'to fashion.' The body is fashioned upon the self by avidyā — it is not the self's native form. Gauḍīya doctrine: the soul's native form is its svarūpa, its eternal Kṛṣṇa-related body in Vaikuṇṭha-Vraja.
    This material body, which has a beginning and an end, is composed of the physical elements, the senses and the modes of nature. The body, imposed on the self by material ignorance, causes one to experience the cycle of birth and death.
    Purport

    The material body, composed of various material qualities, elements and so on, attracts and repels the conditioned soul and thus entangles him in material existence. Because of our attraction and repulsion for our own body and other bodies, we establish temporary relationships, dedicate ourselves to great endeavors and sacrifices, concoct imaginary religions, make noble speeches and thoroughly involve ourselves in material illusion. As Shakespeare said, “All the world’s a stage.” Beyond the somewhat absurd theater of material existence is the real and meaningful world of Kṛṣṇa consciousness, the liberated life of pure souls devoted in loving service to the Supreme Lord.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    This material body, which has a beginning and an end, is composed of the physical elements, the senses and the modes of nature. The body, imposed on the self by material ignorance, causes one to experience the cycle of birth and death.
    Commentary

    The body is also not the jiva. That which you think is to be protected because he is a relative, or to be killed because he is an enemy is simply the body which is subject to birth and death. That body has three aspects: adhibhuta (dravya), the senses or adhyatma (prana), and adhidaivam (guna). It is produced for the jiva by ignorance and causes the jiva to rotate in bodies, under the control of attraction and repulsion.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    This is explained by Śrīdhara Svāmī. Dravya is the adhibhūta (tanmātrās or sense objects and gross elements). Prāṇa is the adhyātmā or senses. Guṇa means the adhidaiva or sense devatās. There is another explanation. Prāṇa refers to action. Guṇa refers to the sense objects like form and taste. Another meaning is that this verse explains the cause of absorption in the present circumstances. The body of Rukmī (eṣaḥ dehah) has a beginning and end etc.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    “Since the body is unconscious, how can it have a peaceful nature? How does the jīva, an aṁśa of the Lord, attain saṁsāra by attaining bodies?” This body, visible with various changes, or this body made of five elements (eṣaḥ), is distinct from the spiritual body of the Lord’s associates. Qualities like peacefulness manifest because it possesses conscious senses. How can the senses be conscious? They are imposed on the self (ātmani): the senses are related to the ātmā which is conscious, which is basis of the senses. This body has birth and death. This body makes the jīva who thinks he is the body become subject to saṁsāra. This takes place by ignorance. Thus it is false.

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    The body is composed of physical elements, senses, and the three modes — and is imposed on the self by ignorance, like a coat thrown over a man in the dark which he then mistakes for his skin. Balarāma's anatomy lecture serves karuṇā: if Rukmiṇī sees Rukmī as a soul wearing a coat, her grief for the coat will loosen.

    Important Words
    • ātmanaḥ — for the self
      Genitive of ātman. The verse-subject. The Bhāgavatam keeps the word ātmā doing double-duty: the individual self (jīvātmā) and the Supreme Self (Paramātmā). Both share the sun-quality of being non-contacted yet illuminating.
    • saṁyogaḥ — contact
      Sam (with) + yoga (joining). What the soul does NOT have with material objects. Yet the same word, in another context, names yoga itself. Balarāma's grammar: there is no saṁyoga at the material level; there can be saṁyoga at the bhakti level (yukta-vairāgya).
    • asataḥ — with that which is insubstantial
      From a- + sat. The 'unreal' — the temporary. Cf. BG 2.16: 'nāsato vidyate bhāvo.' The categorical contrast between sat (the eternal) and asat (the temporary). The soul belongs to sat; the body, to asat.
    • raveḥ — of the sun
      Genitive of ravi. The chapter has been steeped in solar imagery (v. 44 jyotis, here ravi). Solar imagery in Bhāgavatam is rarely impersonal — Sūrya is one of the dvādaśādityas, a personal devatā. The 'sun' here is metaphor, but tinged with personality.
    • sati — O discriminating one
      Feminine vocative of sat. Balarāma calls Rukmiṇī by her ontological category — she who really IS. The same root she possesses (satī, v. 32) is reaffirmed. Her existence is grounded in sat; her grief, in mistaking sat for asat.
    O intelligent lady, the soul never undergoes contact with or separation from insubstantial, material objects, because the soul is their very origin and illuminator. Thus the soul resembles the sun, which neither comes in contact with nor separates from the sense of sight and what is seen.
    Purport

    As explained in the previous text, the conditioned soul ignorantly assumes himself to be the material body and thus rotates in the cycle of birth and death. In fact, matter and spirit are co-energies of the original source of everything, the Supreme Lord, who is the Absolute Truth. As Lord Kṛṣṇa explains in the Bhagavad-gītā (7.5) , jīva-bhūtāṁ mahā-bāho yayedaṁ dhāryate jagat. The material world is sustained by the living beings’ desire to exploit it. The material world is like a prison. Criminals are determined to commit crimes, and thus the government finds it necessary to maintain a prison system. Similarly, the Supreme Lord maintains the material universes because the conditioned souls are determined to rebel against Him and try to enjoy without His loving cooperation. Thus here the phrase tad-dhetutvāt is used to describe the soul, meaning that the soul is the cause of matter assembling itself into a material body. The term tat-prasiddheḥ indicates that the soul is the cause of the body’s being perceived, and the same term also indicates that this fact is well known to the enlightened. Besides its given meaning, the word ātmanaḥ in this verse may indicate the Supreme Soul, in which case the term tad-dhetutvāt indicates that Lord Kṛṣṇa expands His personal potency and thus manifests the material universe. Since the Lord exists eternally in His pure, spiritual body, He never becomes material, as indicated here.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    O intelligent lady, the soul never undergoes contact with or separation from insubstantial, material objects, because the soul is their very origin and illuminator. Thus the soul resembles the sun, which neither comes in contact with nor separates from the sense of sight and what is seen.
    Commentary

    Because the atma is covered by the body, the body is perceived as the atma. Actually however, the atma is not affected by the body. Nor is the paramatma affected by the jiva. First this verse can be explained as referring to the jivatma and matter. There is no permanent contact of the soul with the material body which is impermanent, having a beginning and end. Because there is no contact then there is no separation. How does this take place? The jivatama acts as the source of manifestation of the body. Because the jiva is the manifester of the material body, it is not contaminated by it. How can the manifester be contaminated by that which it manifests? Referring to paramatma and jiva, the verse can be explained as follows. The paramatma (atmanah) has no contact with the jiva (anena) or his impermanent body (asata), because the paramatma is the source of manifestation of the jiva and his body by his very nature as God. Paramatma is never contaminated by either the jiva or the body manifested from him. The manifester is never contaminated by the manifested. In both cases, the example of the sun applies.The sun has no contamination from the eye or form manifested from it. The sun is the paramatma, the eye is the jiva and the form is the body.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The jīva has no connection with matter. Consequently it has no disconnection with matter. It has no connection with matter because in the three phases of time, jīva does not touch (asataḥ) matter. The reason is given. The jīva is the cause of matter’s energy (prasiddheḥ) since it is has a consciousness. If that is so, how can the jīva touch matter? An example is given. The sun, a devatā by birth, unfailing during day and night, does not have connection or disconnection with the eye (sense organ) and form (sense object), the two śaktis which reveal or hide the sun, since it never contacts them. O intelligent Rukmiṇī (sati)! There is another meaning. Let that be! Since you are the eternal Lakṣmī of Kṛṣṇa, you have no relationship with Rukmī. Then he speaks this verse. You (ātmanaḥ) have no connection or disconnection with Rukmī. “Why is this not well known?” You are the supreme Lakṣmī, the cause. Lakṣmī has fame because of your form. She becomes famous from the power of your glance when you appear on earth. “If I am related to him, why do I have no connection or disconnection with him?” Then the example of the sun, eye and form is given.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    First a logical example is given. There is no separation from the body or senses (anyena). Since the separation depends on a previous connection, connection is also non-existent. The previous verse stated that the body was imposed on the ātmā. Thus the body is also false. O pure woman! You have no relationship with purity or impurity. An example is given. The sun has no relation with or separation from the eye or form. Why? The sun is the cause of form and the eye just as the ātmā is the cause of the senses. Being the effects they are negated. Thus they do not exist: they have a beginning and end.

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    The soul resembles the sun — which neither comes in contact with nor separates from sight and the seen, yet illuminates both. Balarāma's analogy is the most refined statement in the chapter: the ātmā is the precondition of all relation, never reducible to a term within relation. Like the sun's relation to a painting — it makes the painting visible without being one of the colors.

    Important Words
    • kalānām — of the phases
      Genitive plural of kalā. A kalā is a sixteenth-portion of the moon. The Bhāgavatam will use the same word for partial incarnations (kalā-avatāra) — phases of the Lord's full disc. Here, phases of the body, never of the soul.
    • indoḥ — of the moon
      Genitive of indu. Soma — the moon. In Bhāgavata cosmology, Soma is also the source of the gandharva-juice and the food of pitṛs. Balarāma chooses the moon because its 'death' is the most popular astronomical illusion.
    • kuhūḥ — the new-moon day
      Kuhū — the dark of the moon. The day when the moon is invisible. Even kuhū is not death — it is invisibility. Balarāma re-trains Rukmiṇī's vocabulary: what looks like brother's death is brother's invisibility-to-her at this moment of crisis.
    • vikriyāḥ — transformations
      Plural of vikriyā. Vi (apart) + kriyā (action). 'Modifications.' In Sāṅkhya, vikāra is a technical term for modification of prakṛti. Balarāma uses vikriyā loosely synonymous — the body undergoes vikriyā; the soul does not.
    • mṛtiḥ — death
      From √mṛ. The bare noun for death. Balarāma uses the technical word and then dissolves it: there is no mṛti of the self, only kalā-vikriyā of the body. Cf. BG 2.20, 'na jāyate mriyate vā kadācit.'
    Birth and other transformations are undergone by the body but never by the self, just as change occurs for the moon’s phases but never for the moon, though the new-moon day may be called the moon’s “death.”
    Purport

    Lord Balarāma here explains how the conditioned souls identify with the body and how this identification should be given up. Certainly every ordinary person considers himself or herself young, middle-aged or old, healthy or sick. But such identification is an illusion, just as the waxing and waning of the moon is an illusion. When we identify ourselves with the material body, we lose our power to understand the soul.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Birth and other transformations are undergone by the body but never by the self, just as change occurs for the moon's phases but never for the moon, though the new-moon day may be called the moon's "death."
    Commentary

    Since the soul has no contact with birth and death, these must only be characteristics of the body. But how can that be, for the awareness of being born, being a child, of aging, is a perception of the self or soul, not the body. This is explained with an example. Just as there are birth and other many phases of the moon, but these is no the birth of the moon which has unlimited phases, and just as the new moon phase is not the death of the moon, so we talk about death of the self, but actually it is death of the body connected with the soul.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The moon, said to be a shadow of the sun and a disk of water, gradually increases and decreases in its phases. But it is always the moon. This is the comparison with the ātmā which remains while the body changes. There is another meaning. “Since I have been born in this family, why connection and disconnection with family members not occur for me?” If changes do not exist for the ātmā, what can be said of you, the svarūpa-śakti of the Lord, with a form of eternity, knowledge and bliss?

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Birth of the body is illustrated. Birth, existence, growth, change, decay and death are six transformations (vikriyā) of the body. Even perfected persons as a pastime sometimes manifest these changes. “The body, using the senses, definitely undergoes these changes, being non different from changes in one’s father etc. But the ātmā also dies at death since it appears that there is no consciousness.” There is even death of the moon. It seems that moon is destroyed since one does not see its disk at the dark moon phase. At other times it seems that the moon is born and undergoes changes because one can see the moon. Similarly the body, not having consciousness, dies at death but not the ātmā. Or “At the dark moon there seems to be death of the moon, since the moon is not present.” The destruction of the phases of the moon is apparent death. It is not real death.

    Analogy

    The moon does not die on the new-moon night; only its phases vanish. Birth and death belong to the body's phases, never to the soul. Balarāma's lunar image is perfect: we say 'the moon has died' on amāvāsyā, but no Sanskrit astronomer believes the moon has ceased to exist. So with the self.

    Important Words
    • śayānaḥ — a sleeping person
      Present participle of √śī. The same root as v. 26 śayīthāḥ — to lie down. Lying down = sleeping = saṁsāric ignorance. Vyāsa's verbal economy is tight.
    • viṣayān — sense objects
      Plural of viṣaya. The objects of the senses — sound, touch, form, taste, smell. In Gauḍīya texts viṣaya often means 'object of enjoyment as opposed to its enjoyer' — Kṛṣṇa is the only true viṣayī, the only one for whom viṣaya is appropriate.
    • abudhaḥ — the unintelligent
      A- (not) + budha (wise). One who does not budh — does not awaken. The same root as buddha. Balarāma names the materially-conditioned as still-asleep. Bhakti is the awakening that this verse points toward.
    • asati arthe — in that which is not real
      Locative: asat (unreal) + artha (object/aim). The dream-content is asat. Yet experience occurs in it. The verse opens the space for the Bhāgavata to distinguish vyavahāra-sat (transactional reality) from pāramārthika-sat (ultimate reality).
    • anubhuṅkte — experiences
      Present middle of anu-√bhuj. To experience-after, to enjoy. Note: even in dream, one anubhuṅkte. The verb is real; only its object is asat. Bhakti redirects the same anubhava — toward Kṛṣṇa, who is sat.
    As a sleeping person perceives himself, the objects of sense enjoyment and the fruits of his acts within the illusion of a dream, so one who is unintelligent undergoes material existence.
    Purport

    As stated in śruti, asaṅgo hy ayaṁ puruṣaḥ: “The living being has no intimate connection with the material world.” This point is explained in the present verse. A similar statement is found in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (11.22.56) : arthe ’hy avidyamāne ’pi saṁsṛtir na nivartate dhyāyato viṣayān asya svapne ’narthāgamo yathā “For one who is meditating on sense gratification, material life, although lacking factual existence, does not go away, just as the unpleasant experiences of a dream do not.”

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    As a sleeping person perceives himself, the objects of sense enjoyment and the fruits of his acts within the illusion of a dream, so one who is unintelligent undergoes material existence.
    Commentary

    From the sruti statement "asango’ yam purusah" it is understood that the atma is actually not contaminated by the body, and material life exists only because of the conception of body due to ignorance with its inconceivable energy. This is illustrated with an example. Though objects themselves are real, while sleeping a person may experience objects such as countries to be conquered with vast armies, results such as victory, and enjoyment of the results such as sandalwood and women. And sometimes he experiences defeat, bondage, beating and abuse. In this way, the unintelligent person experiences in an unreal way the world of happiness and distress due to association with the body.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    A sleeping person experiences objects and fruits as if in the waking state (anu—bhuṅkte). He experiences himself, seeing himself as a king etc. There is another meaning. “If this is so, why do does Rukmī seem to be absorbed in his nature, even after hearing the truth?” Rukmī, a fool, simply undergoes saṁsāra, just as a sleeping person experiences objects in a dream.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    An example is given to show the falsity of saṁsāra by ātmā’s identification with body under ignorance. A sleeping person, any person, seeing a dream (śayānaḥ), experiences (bhuṅkte) objects and results (happiness and suffering), similar to the waking state (anu) and in the dream sees himself (ātmanam) as a king etc. “If this is so, then everything is real in the dream.” No. They are non-existent. The objects (arthe) are non-existent (asati). The person who does not know about ātmā (abudhaḥ) undergoes saṁsāra (bhavam). From ignorance arises birth and death. It has no real existence.

    Atma
    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    A sleeping man perceives himself, sense-objects, and the fruits of acts inside a dream — all real to him while dreaming, all unreal upon waking. Balarāma's image is one of the Vedānta's classic prasthāna; in Gauḍīya hands it becomes the diagnosis from which bhakti is the awakening, not jñāna alone.

    Stories
    Caitanya's mahā-bhāva and the awakening of the dreamer

    Caitanya-caritāmṛta describes mahā-bhāva not as escape from the dream but as the discovery, while still dreaming, that the dream is also Kṛṣṇa-līlā — that the same forms one once mistook for self-and-other are, properly seen, manifestations of the Lord's energy.

    Gauḍīyas thus read SB 10.54.48 not as a counsel to dis-relate from the dream, but to re-relate — to wake INTO Kṛṣṇa-consciousness, where the same world becomes the field of bhakti rather than the field of viṣaya. The dream is not refuted; it is re-cast.
